abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the clinical and echocardiographic outcomes of transcatheter tricuspid annuloplasty using the Cardioband system in a single-center cohort of high-risk patients with severe functional tricuspid regurgitation.
METHODS: This single-center prospective cohort study included 64 consecutive patients with severe functional tricuspid regurgitation undergoing transcatheter tricuspid annuloplasty with the Cardioband system. Clinical and echocardiographic data were collected at baseline, discharge, 6-months, and 12-months. Primary endpoints included changes in tricuspid regurgitation severity, annular dimensions, and clinical status, as well as all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalization. Outcomes were analyzed using available-case data.
RESULTS: At 12-months, among patients with available echocardiographic data (n = 44), tricuspid regurgitation severity was reduced compared with baseline (p < 0.001); 15.9% had trace or mild TR, 45.5% had moderate TR, 27.3% had severe TR, and 11.4% had massive or torrential TR. All-cause mortality at 12-months was 6.3% (4/64 patients). According to TVARC criteria, intraprocedural success was achieved in 81.3% of patients, while a more stringent definition yielded a success rate of 65.6%.
CONCLUSION: In this single-center cohort of high-risk patients with severe functional tricuspid regurgitation, transcatheter tricuspid annuloplasty using the Cardioband system was associated with reductions in tricuspid regurgitation severity and improvements in selected clinical parameters at 12-months. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution given the observational design, incomplete follow-up, and the absence of a control group, as well as the observed rate of procedural complications. Further studies, ideally including larger multicenter cohorts and controlled comparisons, are needed to better define the role of this therapy in the management of tricuspid regurgitation.
title: Clinical outcomes and coronary complication risk after transcatheter tricuspid annuloplasty with cardioband: a 12-month single-center cohort study.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with drug-eluting stents has been widely used to treat patients with left main coronary artery disease; however, long-term comparative outcomes versus coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) in real-world populations remain poorly characterised. We aimed to compare long-term all-cause mortality after PCI or CABG in Asian patients with unprotected left main coronary artery disease.
METHODS: We analysed prospectively collected data from the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry, conducted at 46 hospitals in South Korea, India, Japan, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The registry enrolled adults aged 18 years or older with unprotected left main coronary artery disease (defined as a stenosis diameter of ≥50% as visually estimated on angiography), who had been treated with PCI, CABG, or medical therapy alone. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. We used a target trial emulation framework to compare the long-term risk of all-cause mortality between PCI with drug-eluting stents and isolated CABG. We used propensity-score overlap weighting to adjust for measured baseline covariates. The IRIS-MAIN Registry study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01341327).
FINDINGS: Between Jan 1, 2003, and Dec 31, 2024, 6900 patients were enrolled in the IRIS-MAIN registry, of whom 5379 (78·0%) underwent coronary revascularisation through either PCI with drug-eluting stents (3836 [71·3%]) or CABG (1543 [28·7%]) and were included in the analysis. The median duration of follow-up for all patients was 10·0 years (IQR 5·0-16·7). In the overlap-weighted population, no statistically detectable difference in 10-year weighted Kaplan-Meier rates of all-cause mortality was observed between PCI and CABG (24·0% vs 22·9%; overlap-weighted hazard ratio 1·00 [95% CI 0·87-1·14]; p=0·99). The confidence interval does not exclude a mortality benefit or harm with either strategy.
INTERPRETATION: In this non-randomised registry analysis of patients with left main coronary artery disease, there was no statistically detectable difference in all-cause mortality between PCI and CABG. For patients considered suitable for either strategy, multidisciplinary Heart Team discussion might help patients and clinicians weigh potential trade-offs in the choice between PCI and CABG. These findings are observational and cannot establish causal treatment effects or equivalence in survival.
FUNDING: The CardioVascular Research Foundation (South Korea).

appraisal.design_and_n: Non-randomised registry analysis with target trial emulation; 5379 patients underwent coronary revascularisation through either PCI with drug-eluting stents (3836 [71·3%]) or CABG (1543 [28·7%]); median follow-up 10·0 years.
appraisal.main_limitation: Observational design with adjustment for measured covariates only; the authors state that the confidence interval does not exclude benefit or harm with either strategy and that equivalence cannot be established.
appraisal.one_line: Target trial emulation in the IRIS-MAIN registry found no statistically detectable difference in 10-year all-cause mortality between PCI with drug-eluting stents and CABG for unprotected left main disease in Asian patients.
appraisal.primary_result_as_reported: In the overlap-weighted population, no statistically detectable difference in 10-year weighted Kaplan-Meier rates of all-cause mortality was observed between PCI and CABG (24·0% vs 22·9%; overlap-weighted hazard ratio 1·00 [95% CI 0·87-1·14]; p=0·99).
appraisal.why_it_matters: Large long-term emulated-trial comparison for left main disease in a general-tier journal; informs the PCI versus CABG debate but covers all ages and Asian registries, not the older-patient population of Q-004.

register_verdicts.note: Left main PCI versus CABG in a mostly Asian all-age registry; does not address patients aged 75 and over in national registries, though it is a methodological precedent.

title: Long-term outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention with drug-eluting stents versus coronary artery bypass grafting for left main coronary artery disease: a prospective analysis of the multicentre IRIS-MAIN registry.

abstract: Long-term data on transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (TEER) for significant mitral regurgitation (MR) remain limited. We aimed to evaluate long-term clinical outcomes and functional and echocardiographic findings during follow-up after MitraClip in a long-term subanalysis of the prospective multicenter GIOTTO registry. We included 406 consecutive patients undergoing MitraClip implantation for significant MR from 6 Italian centers contributing long-term follow-up. Baseline, procedural, in-hospital, and long-term follow-up data were compared according to MR etiology. Predictors of all-cause death were assessed using Cox regression analysis. Mean follow-up was 56.4±27.2 months. The cohort included 257 (63.3%) patients with functional or mixed MR and 149 (36.7%) with degenerative MR, who were older, more often female, and had smaller ventricles and higher LVEF, whereas functional or mixed MR patients had greater ischemic burden, conduction disease, prior revascularization, pacemaker implantation, and ventricular remodeling. During the overall observation period, crude all-cause death occurred in 161 patients (39.7%) and MVARC-style cardiovascular death in 98 (24.1%), without significant differences between groups. Mitral surgery, repeat TEER, endocarditis, and stroke occurred in 2.2%, 0.7%, 1.5%, and 3.5%, respectively. Among patients with available follow-up assessment, 77.5% were in NYHA class I/II. At the actual 5-year landmark echocardiographic assessment, 82.9% had none or mild MR and 97.1% had no more than moderate MR. Independent mortality predictors were older age, lower body mass index, right bundle branch block, MR etiology, larger LV end-systolic diameter, higher systolic pulmonary artery pressure, and longer index hospitalization (all p <0.05). In conclusion, in this prospective multicenter cohort, TEER with MitraClip in high-risk patients was associated with high procedural success and favorable long-term clinical and echocardiographic findings among patients with available follow-up. Mortality appeared to be associated with patient vulnerability, MR etiology, ventricular remodeling, pulmonary hypertension, and the early post-procedural course.
title: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair for mitral valve regurgitation: insights from a 5-year prospective multicenter registry.
Very low gradient aortic stenosis: the black sheep of TAVI, but do these patients still benefit?

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Major adverse cardiovascular events arising from non-culprit lesions (NCLs) remain relevant in patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS), highlighting the need for more effective identification of vulnerable plaques. Although several coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA)-derived high-risk features are recognized as markers of plaque vulnerability, the significance of soft plaque morphology remains unclear. This study investigated whether ACS is associated with soft plaque morphology in NCLs on CCTA.
METHODS AND RESULTS: Overall, 174 NCLs from 69 patients with ACS or chronic coronary syndrome (CCS) who underwent CCTA within 1 month of percutaneous coronary intervention were analyzed. Soft plaques were classified according to the presence or absence of focal soft plaque thickening (FSPT), defined as localized thickening of the soft plaque component measuring ≥500 μm in at least one cross-sectional slice. Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) was co-registered with CCTA in 49 lesions. The soft plaque burden did not differ significantly between NCLs in patients with ACS and CCS, whereas FSPT was more frequently observed in NCLs in patients with ACS (56.4% vs. 18.8%; p < 0.001). In multivariable analysis accounting for within-patient clustering, ACS was independently associated with FSPT (odds ratio, 6.09; 95% confidence interval, 2.72-13.60; p < 0.001). On co-registered IVUS, lesions with FSPT showed larger attenuation arcs and more frequent superficial attenuation.
CONCLUSIONS: ACS was independently associated with CCTA-derived FSPT in NCLs. These exploratory findings suggest that morphological assessment of soft plaques on CCTA may provide complementary information for the characterization of NCLs. Further validation in independent cohorts is warranted.
title: Distinct soft plaque morphology on coronary computed tomography angiography in non-culprit lesions among patients with acute coronary syndrome.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an established genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Whether elevated Lp(a) identifies a broader phenotype of aggressive coronary disease, integrating anatomical disease burden and recurrent clinical manifestations, remains incompletely characterised.
METHODS: We analysed 1892 patients with coronary artery disease from the multicentre CERES cohort after exclusion of myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA). Lp(a) was analysed continuously, after natural-log transformation, and categorically using >50 mg/dL. Multivariable logistic regression models were adjusted for age, sex, hypertension, diabetes, smoking, and historical maximum LDL cholesterol (LDL-C).
RESULTS: Lp(a) was available in 1833 patients; median concentration was 24.7 [9.1-63.7] mg/dL, and 33.2% had Lp(a) >50 mg/dL. Multivessel disease was present in 50.4% and recurrent coronary events in 19.5%. Lp(a) was independently associated with multivessel disease (OR, 1.004; 95% CI, 1.001-1.006; p = 0.002) and recurrent coronary events (OR, 1.004; 95% CI, 1.001-1.006; p = 0.003). Lp(a) >50 mg/dL was associated with multivessel disease (OR, 1.406; 95% CI, 1.144-1.730; p = 0.001) and recurrent events (OR, 1.504; 95% CI, 1.166-1.942; p = 0.002).
CONCLUSIONS: Elevated Lp(a) was independently associated with greater anatomical coronary disease burden and recurrent coronary events, supporting its role as a marker of an aggressive coronary disease phenotype.
title: Lipoprotein(a) and an aggressive coronary disease phenotype: Association with multivessel disease and recurrent coronary events in the CERES study.

abstract: Early gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) cancer commonly presents without distant disease. The development of locoregional lymphadenopathy and acute pulmonary embolism raises concern for metastatic disease and may lead to inappropriate upstaging if not properly investigated. We present a 51-year-old immunocompetent Hispanic man with newly diagnosed T1a GEJ adenocarcinoma who developed FDG-avid mediastinal lymphadenopathy and an incidental subsegmental pulmonary embolism on staging computed tomography. Histological sampling via endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration revealed granulomatous inflammation without malignancy. Further workup confirmed an acute Coccidioides lymphadenitis. The patient was successfully treated with fluconazole 400 mg daily for three months, with complete radiological and endoscopic resolution. This case underscores the critical importance of histological confirmation of lymphadenopathy before attributing it to metastatic disease in early-stage GEJ cancer. Failure to consider infectious etiologies, particularly coccidioidomycosis in endemic areas or in patients with travel history, may result in unnecessary upstaging, inappropriate treatment escalation, and avoidable harm.
journal: Revista de gastroenterologia del Peru : organo oficial de la Sociedad de Gastroenterologia del Peru
title: From presumed metastasis to infection: coccidioidomycosis mimicking metastatic gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma.

abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism (PE) is a potentially life-threatening condition that can precipitate obstructive shock, a form of circulatory failure caused by the mechanical obstruction of blood flow through the pulmonary circulation. This article explores the pathophysiological mechanisms linking massive PE to obstructive shock, highlighting key diagnostic challenges, and the importance of rapid recognition in the emergency setting. We examine current strategies for risk stratification, imaging, and laboratory testing, as well as emerging biomarkers that may aid in early identification. The article also evaluates the efficacy and limitations of therapeutic interventions, including systemic thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapies, and surgical embolectomy, in the context of hemodynamic instability. Understanding the complex interplay between PE and obstructive shock is essential for optimizing outcomes in critically ill patients.
title: Pathophysiology of Right Ventricular Failure in Pulmonary Embolism.

abstract: Acute pulmonary embolism remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, with prognosis determined by right ventricular (RV) adaptation to the abrupt rise in pulmonary vascular resistance. Although most cases can be managed outside the intensive care unit, patients with RV failure, hemodynamic instability, or cardiac arrest require advanced monitoring and intervention. Management in this setting emphasizes rapid diagnosis and risk stratification, timely initiation of reperfusion therapies, and carefully tailored hemodynamic and respiratory support. Optimal outcomes rely on multidisciplinary collaboration, early escalation of care, and individualized, evidence-based decision-making.
title: Intensive Care Unit Management of the Hemodynamically Significant Pulmonary Embolism.

abstract: Catheter-directed therapies, including catheter-directed thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy, are increasingly used in patients with intermediate and high-risk pulmonary embolism. Complications, such as bleeding, vascular injury, and hemodynamic instability, require diligent preprocedural planning involving bailout strategies and the potential for extracorporeal support. We provide a pragmatic framework for appropriate patient selection of catheter-directed treatment. Although randomized data remain limited, ongoing pivotal trials will help clarify appropriate patient selection and clinical efficacy compared to anticoagulation and systemic thrombolysis alone.
title: Catheter-directed Treatment of Pulmonary Embolism.

abstract: This article summarizes the evolution of pulmonary embolism therapy, from early heparin use and landmark thrombolysis trials to modern catheter-based therapies, including catheter-directed thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy. It reviews how advancements in medical and device therapies have shaped treatment selection while highlighting persistent evidence gaps. Across decades of trials, the primary challenge remains achieving balance between effective reperfusion with optimization of safety outcomes and clinical benefit.
title: Trials Review.

abstract: Pulmonary embolism is a life-threatening condition requiring prompt anticoagulation to prevent clot propagation and recurrence. Risk stratification guides therapy, with systemic thrombolysis reserved for high-risk patients and selected intermediate-high risk cases due to significant bleeding risk. Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred for most low and intermediate-low risk patients, while low-molecular-weight heparin and unfractionated heparin remain critical for higher- risk or procedurally complex cases. Emerging strategies including low-dose thrombolysis, catheter-directed therapies, and the future use of Factor XI inhibitors may improve safety without compromising efficacy. Management of bleeding complications necessitates rapid intervention, reversal when available, and coordinated multidisciplinary care.
title: Anticoagulation and Thrombolysis.

abstract: Surgical pulmonary embolectomy was once considered a salvage procedure in patients who were dying or dead. Improvements in surgical technique, technologies, and patient selection mean that surgical embolectomy is a safe procedure, potentially more effective than thrombolytics or percutaneous thrombectomy procedures. The specific patient populations who may benefit most from surgical embolectomy are discussed. The surgical technique, using cardiopulmonary bypass, is described in detail. Special situations such as clots in transit, pregnant patients with pulmonary embolism, and the emerging role of mechanical circulatory support in the management of this condition are also discussed.
title: Surgical Management of Pulmonary Embolism.

abstract: Clot in transit, defined as a mobile right heart thrombus, is a rare but life-threatening manifestation of venous thromboembolism. Its presence in acute pulmonary embolism is associated with high mortality and hemodynamic instability. Diagnosis relies primarily on echocardiography, with adjunctive roles for computed tomography and cardiac magnetic resonance. Management remains challenging due to the absence of randomized trials. Treatment options include anticoagulation alone, systemic thrombolysis, surgical embolectomy, and catheter-based interventions, with outcomes favoring active reperfusion in unstable patients. Multidisciplinary decision-making is essential, and ongoing research aims to clarify optimal strategies to improve survival in this high-risk population.
title: Clot in Transit.

abstract: This article highlights the limitations of thrombolysis in high-risk pulmonary embolism and the emerging role of temporary mechanical circulatory support, especially venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, as a bridge to recovery or definitive therapy. The pathophysiology of right ventricular failure in pulmonary embolism, risk stratification strategies, and decision-making frameworks for initiating mechanical circulatory support are reviewed. Further, we cover practical considerations, including device selection, circuit management during thrombectomy, and the imperative for preanesthesia planning in risk mitigation. Finally, this article highlights the importance of conducting prospective and randomized studies on device choice, timing, and integration with reperfusion strategies.
title: Temporary Mechanical Circulatory Support in Pulmonary Embolism.

abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common concern in the Emergency Department (ED) and has a wide variety of presentations. The initial stage of ED workup involves the calculation of pretest probability, using a clinical calculator or experienced clinician gestalt, and then progresses to diagnostic testing, which may involve D-Dimer measurement or radiographic imaging (typically computed tomography and ultrasonography). Management of PE depends primarily on the function of the right ventricle and the presence of shock. Low-risk PEs can be treated with outpatient oral anticoagulation, while patients who are in shock should undergo systemic thrombolysis.
title: Emergency Department Management of Acute Pulmonary Embolism.

abstract: Cor triatriatum sinister is an exceptionally rare congenital cardiac anomaly [1]. While restrictive forms are typically present in infancy or early childhood, survival into adolescence with a 2-3 mm fenestration is unusual [2, 3]. We report a 14-year-old male, misdiagnosed with refractory asthma for years, who presented with palpitations. Imaging and catheterisation revealed severe post-capillary pulmonary hypertension with echocardiographic evidence of right-sided chamber dilatation, D-shaped left ventricular configuration, moderate tricuspid regurgitation, and an estimated pulmonary artery pressure of 85 mmHg. Cardiac catheterisation showed PA pressure of 50/30 mmHg (mean 39 mmHg), PCWP of 28 mmHg, Qp/Qs of 1.14, and a favourable PVR/SVR ratio of 0.12, indicating reversibility. Successful surgical resection of a calcified membrane was performed via right anterolateral thoracotomy. This case underscores the importance of considering cor triatriatum sinister in adolescents with unexplained respiratory symptoms or wheezing and highlights the value of correlating echocardiographic evidence of obstruction with invasive haemodynamic assessment before surgery [4, 5].
title: A rare late presentation of restrictive cor triatriatum sinister in a 14-year-old male mimicking refractory asthma.

abstract: Fulminant myocarditis is a life-threatening inflammatory cardiac syndrome characterized by severe myocardial injury and abrupt deterioration of cardiac function, leading to rapidly progressive cardiogenic shock. Patients often require intravenous vasoactive therapy and/or temporary mechanical circulatory support to maintain systemic perfusion and prevent multiorgan failure. Although frequently preceded by a viral prodrome and affecting young and healthy individuals, fulminant myocarditis encompasses diverse etiologies, including immune-mediated and toxin-related subtypes, with major implications for diagnosis and treatment. Optimal management relies on early recognition, prompt admission to specialized cardiac intensive care units, and rapid access to advanced diagnostics, including endomyocardial biopsy and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, to confirm myocardial inflammation, exclude ischemic disease, and guide etiology-directed therapy. Hemodynamic stabilization requires tailored use of vasopressors and inotropes while minimizing catecholamine-related arrhythmias and myocardial oxygen demand. For refractory shock, early escalation to temporary mechanical circulatory support, most commonly venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, is central to restore perfusion and provide a bridge to recovery or advanced therapy. Because fulminant myocarditis frequently involves malignant arrhythmias and multiorgan dysfunction, integrated critical care management is essential. This review summarizes a practical intensive care approach to fulminant myocarditis, emphasizing early diagnosis, individualized hemodynamic and device-based support, multiorgan management, and phenotype-driven immunomodulatory treatment strategies.
journal: Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia
title: Critical Care Management of Patients With Acute Fulminant Myocarditis.

abstract: Drug-coated balloons (DCBs) are widely used in clinical practice; however, the clinical impact of differences between DCB platforms, including paclitaxel dose, remains uncertain. This study compared the clinical efficacy and safety of low-dose (LD) versus regular-dose (RD) paclitaxel-coated balloons (PCBs) for de novo coronary lesions using data from the ALLIANCE registry, a prospective, multicenter, all-comers study. Patients treated with an LD-PCB (AGENT) or RD-PCB (SeQuent Please Neo) were compared using propensity score matching at a target LD-to-RD ratio of 2:1. The primary endpoint was 1-year target lesion failure (TLF), defined as a composite of cardiac death, target vessel myocardial infarction, and clinically driven target lesion revascularization (cd-TLR). Among 1,568 patients included in this analysis, propensity score matching yielded 784 patients in the LD-PCB group and 419 in the RD-PCB group. At 1 year, the incidence of TLF was 5.1% in the LD-PCB group and 3.8% in the RD-PCB group (p = 0.33). Kaplan-Meier analyses showed no significant between-group differences in TLF or its individual components. In this propensity score-matched registry analysis, LD-PCBs and RD-PCBs were associated with no statistically significant difference in 1-year TLF. These findings are exploratory and hypothesis-generating and do not establish equivalence between the two platforms.
title: Low-dose versus regular-dose paclitaxel-coated balloons for de novo coronary lesions: the ALLIANCE registry.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mixed aortic valve disease (MAVD), defined as the coexistence of significant aortic stenosis (AS) and aortic regurgitation (AR), presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Prior studies rarely distinguished bicuspid valve morphology in MAVD populations, and no study has evaluated long-term transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) outcomes between bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) and tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) patients in this setting. The aim is to investigate the clinical outcomes of BAV versus TAV morphology in patients with MAVD undergoing TAVR.
METHODS: Between March 2013 and December 2024, 610 MAVD patients undergoing TAVR were included. Patients with severe AS and concomitant presence of moderate or more severe aortic regurgitation were defined as the MAVD. Clinical outcomes, functional status and echocardiography were followed and compared.
RESULTS: A total of 610 patients were included in this study, 220 (36.1%) of whom were BAV morphology. BAV patients were younger (73 vs. 75 years, p < 0.001) and had a lower Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score (3.47% vs. 4.15%, p < 0.001) compared to TAV patients. The five-year mortality rate was lower in bicuspid than tricuspid patients (10.5% vs. 18.7%, log-rank p = 0.014), while Cox regression analysis did not indicate BAV as an independent predictor of five-year all-cause mortality after multivariable adjustment (hazard ratio [HR] 0.75, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.47-1.22, p = 0.253). During the one-year follow-up after procedure, BAV patients exhibited a greater increase in AVA and LVEF (p for interaction = 0.012 and 0.011, respectively), and a greater reduction in mean gradient and peak velocity (both p for interaction < 0.001). Meanwhile, similar left ventricular reverse remodelling was found during follow-up (both p for trend < 0.001).
CONCLUSIONS: In MAVD patients undergoing TAVR, bicuspid and tricuspid valve morphologies demonstrated comparable long-term clinical outcomes. BAV patients demonstrated greater improvements in left ventricular function and transvalvular hemodynamics, suggesting that bicuspid morphology itself does not confer an adverse long-term prognostic effect in appropriately selected patients with MAVD undergoing TAVR.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT02803294.
title: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement in bicuspid versus tricuspid aortic valves among patients with mixed aortic valve disease.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aimed to investigate the association between preprocedural frailty and long-term all-cause mortality in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR).
METHODS: A systematic search of PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library was conducted from database inception to 15 February 2026. The methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to pool adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) with their corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Thirteen cohort studies involving 429,827 patients were included in the systematic review. Of these, 8 studies (4,726 patients) reporting comparable adjusted effect estimates were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Preprocedural frailty was associated with a higher risk of long-term all-cause mortality after TAVR (HR = 1.85, 95% CI 1.51-2.25; I² = 39.4%). The association was generally consistent across subgroup analyses stratified by follow-up duration and frailty assessment methodology. Five studies that were not amenable to quantitative pooling because of non-comparable effect formats or data structures showed a concordant direction of effect, with some studies demonstrating a graded relationship between increasing frailty burden and mortality risk.
CONCLUSIONS: Preprocedural frailty is significantly associated with increased long-term all-cause mortality in older adults undergoing TAVR. These findings support the incorporation of frailty assessment into routine preprocedural geriatric risk stratification and multidisciplinary decision-making.
title: Impact of preprocedural frailty on long-term mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

abstract: This retrospective study evaluated the diagnostic screening and early identification value of admission baseline cardiac and renal biomarkers for newly developed in-hospital type 1 cardiorenal syndrome (CRS) after acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Baseline samples were collected at emergency admission before the documented onset of renal injury. A total of 150 AMI patients were included, comprising 60 patients who developed incident CRS and 90 AMI controls without renal impairment. Laboratory indicators included cardiac markers (cardiac troponin I [cTnI] and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide [NT-proBNP]) and renal-related markers including retinol-binding protein (RBP), urea, serum creatinine and spot urinary microalbumin. Multivariate logistic regression adjusted for infarct size, haemodynamic status, baseline renal function, comorbidities and guideline-directed cardiovascular medications, and ROC analysis assessed discriminatory performance. Baseline urea, urinary microalbumin and NT-proBNP were higher, while RBP was lower, in patients who developed CRS (all P < 0.0001). Independently associated indicators included cTnI (OR = 0.628, 95% CI: 0.436-0.903, P = 0.012), RBP (OR = 0.931, 95% CI: 0.883-0.981, P = 0.008), urea (OR = 1.226, 95% CI: 1.039-1.446, P = 0.016) and urinary microalbumin (OR = 1.017, 95% CI: 1.004-1.031, P = 0.013). Urea showed the highest AUC (0.914; sensitivity, 78.5%; specificity, 83.4%). Raw urinary microalbumin showed an AUC of 0.747, and urinary microalbumin showed improved discriminatory performance after urine creatinine calibration and covariate adjustment (AUC = 0.883). Combined assessment of these biomarkers may support diagnostic screening of AMI patients at increased risk of in-hospital CRS.
title: Admission cardiac and renal biomarkers for early identification of type 1 cardiorenal syndrome after acute myocardial infarction.

abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: The long-term prognostic value of a guideline-recommended selective sequential anatomical-functional imaging strategy using coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) followed by quantitative [15O]H2O positron emission tomography (PET) remains uncertain. We evaluated its long-term prognostic value in patients with first symptoms suggestive of obstructive coronary artery disease (CAD).
METHODS: In this multicentre European cohort, symptomatic patients first underwent CCTA and were selectively referred to quantitative [15O]H2O PET in case of suspected obstructive stenosis (≥50%). Patients were stratified according to CCTA findings and PET-derived ischaemia (normal CCTA; non-obstructive CAD on CCTA; obstructive CAD on CCTA without ischaemia; obstructive CAD on CCTA with ischaemia). The primary endpoint was a composite of all-cause mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction (MI), and hospitalization for unstable angina (UA). Adjusted hazard ratios (aHRs) were calculated.
RESULTS: Among 3,918 patients (61.0±9.8 years; 54.3% female) with a median follow-up of 5.1 [3.8-8.0] years, 278 (7.1%) experienced the primary endpoint. aHRs increased stepwise across CCTA-PET categories. Compared to normal CCTA, non-obstructive CAD and obstructive CAD without ischaemia were associated with a higher risk of the combined primary endpoint (aHR 1.89, [95%CI: 1.23-2.91], p=0.004; aHR 3.20, [95%CI: 1.95-5.25], p<0.001). Among patients with obstructive CAD on CCTA, PET-derived ischaemia further increased the risk of the primary endpoint (aHR 1.55, [95%CI: 1.05-2.30]; p=0.029), but not when excluding UA from the composite endpoint (aHR 1.37, [95%CI 0.90-2.07]; p=0.141). PET-derived ischaemia primarily predicted events within the first year, while obstructive CCTA findings remained associated with long-term hard outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS: A sequential strategy combining CCTA and quantitative [15O]H2O PET provides robust and incremental long-term risk stratification. While PET-derived ischaemia refines prediction of short-term and symptom-driven events, CCTA-derived CAD remains the principal determinant of long-term hard outcomes.
title: Long-term Prognostic Value of Sequential Coronary CT Angiography and Quantitative PET in Suspected Chronic Coronary Syndromes: A Multicentre study.

abstract:
PURPOSE: To compare short- and long-term outcomes of bare-metal (BMS) vs covered (CS) balloon-expandable stents in transplant renal artery stenosis (TRAS).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: This retrospective study evaluated patients who underwent elective stent placement for TRAS between 2016 and 2023. Short-term efficacy was assessed by clinical improvement (resolution of resistant hypertension/hypervolemia) and reduction in serum creatinine (sCr) within 14 days post-procedure. Long-term outcomes included Doppler ultrasound parameters - peak systolic velocity (PSV), acceleration time (AT) and resistive index (RI) - and restenosis/occlusion rates requiring or not intervention. Graft survival at the latest follow-up was recorded.
RESULTS: A total of 40 patients (mean age 58 ± 13 years, 68% male) were treated with BMS (n = 31) or CS (n = 9). Clinical improvement was observed in 71% of BMS and 83% of CS patients (P = 1.00). Median sCr decreased by 26% and 33% in BMS and CS patients, respectively (P = .30). At a median follow-up of 29 months, there were no statistically significant differences between groups in median PSV reduction (47% BMS vs 47% CS; P = .44), AT improvement (36% BMS vs 25% CS; P = .38) or RI increase (15% BMS vs 33% CS; P = .12). In the BMS group, 2 cases of in-stent restenosis occurred (6.5%). In the CS group, 1 stent occlusion occurred (11%), resulting in graft loss. At final follow-up, overall graft survival was 85%.
CONCLUSION: In this pilot study, BMS and CS showed no significant differences in TRAS outcomes. Further studies are warranted to better guide stent selection.Clinical ImpactIn transplant renal artery stenosis, balloon-expandable covered stents achieved clinical, biochemical and Doppler outcomes comparable to bare-metal stents, despite being used in more complex, atherosclerotic and longer lesions. This first direct comparison suggests that covered stents may be a reasonable option when heavy calcification, a friable wall or mural thrombus raise concern for embolisation or rupture, while bare-metal stents remain appropriate for most lesions. The single late covered-stent occlusion with graft loss highlights the need for careful platform selection and antiplatelet management. These pilot data should inform adequately powered multicentre registries rather than directly change practice.
journal: Journal of endovascular therapy : an official journal of the International Society of Endovascular Specialists
title: Bare-Metal vs Covered Balloon-Expandable Stents for Transplant Renal Artery Stenosis: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
Transcatheter aortic valve implantation vs surgical replacement in low-risk aortic stenosis: time-dependent late mortality in a pooled analysis of trials.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acute heart failure (AHF) is prone to early clinical deterioration. The prognostic nutritional index (PNI), derived from serum albumin and lymphocyte count, is readily available. We evaluated the association of early PNI with incident in-hospital adverse cardiovascular events and its incremental prognostic value.
METHODS: This retrospective cohort included consecutive adults presenting to the emergency department with AHF from March 2022 through March 2026. PNI was calculated from measurements obtained within 24 h and classified as low (<45) or high (≥45). The primary outcome was a post-index composite of all-cause death, cardiogenic shock, sustained ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, acute myocardial infarction, or worsening AHF requiring treatment escalation. Multivariable logistic regression evaluated associations; missing covariates were handled using multiple imputation. Discrimination was quantified by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC).
RESULTS: Of 367 patients (156 low PNI; 211 high PNI), 112 (30.5%) experienced the primary outcome. Events occurred in 43.6% and 20.9%, respectively (P < 0.001). After adjustment, low PNI remained associated with higher odds of the primary outcome (odds ratio [OR], 1.92; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.10-3.35; P = 0.022). Each 5-point PNI increase was associated with lower odds (OR, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.56-0.90; P = 0.003). PNI alone yielded an AUC of 0.714. Adding PNI increased the conventional model AUC from 0.776 to 0.829 (increase, 0.053; 95% CI, 0.021-0.085; P = 0.001); bootstrap-corrected AUCs were 0.752 and 0.803, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS: Low PNI was associated with higher adjusted odds of in-hospital adverse cardiovascular events. PNI provided modest incremental prognostic information and may serve as a complementary marker for early risk stratification.
title: Association of the prognostic nutritional index with in-hospital adverse cardiovascular events among emergency department patients with acute heart failure.

abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Totally endoscopic mitral valve (MV) surgery is an established therapy for mitral regurgitation (MR) with high repair rates at experienced centers. In certain scenarios, however, repair is not feasible, necessitating chordal-sparing MV replacement. This study investigates the reasons for totally endoscopic MV replacement and reports 5-year outcomes.
METHODS: Between 2012 and 2022, 1,037 consecutive patients underwent totally endoscopic MV surgery. Of those, 75 patients (7.2%) underwent chordal-sparing MV replacement. Preoperative characteristics, periprocedural data, and mid-term outcomes were retrospectively analyzed and compared to a 1:1 propensity score-matched repair group.
RESULTS: After matching, baseline characteristics were balanced. Indications for MV replacement included sclerotic leaflets (28.0%), endocarditis (26.7%), MV stenosis (17.3%), failed repair attempt (17.3%), rheumatic disease (12.0%), and residual MR after transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (7%). Cross-clamp and bypass times were similar. Re-thoracotomy occurred in 14.7% vs. 6.7%, while permanent pacemaker implantation occurred solely after replacement (16.0%). Low cardiac output rates were comparable (6.7% vs. 5.5%). Transvalvular gradients at discharge were higher after replacement (p < 0.001). No paravalvular leakage was observed. In-hospital mortality was 4% vs. 0%. Five-year survival was 86.7% vs. 94.7%, and reintervention rates were similar (4.0% vs. 6.7%).
CONCLUSION: Totally endoscopic MV surgery at a high-volume center is infrequently associated with MV replacement. The main reasons included sclerotic leaflet pathology, MV stenosis, and endocarditis. Despite a higher comorbidity burden and residual baseline imbalance after matching, early and mid-term outcomes were acceptable. Totally endoscopic chordal-sparing MV replacement represents a safe and clinically effective treatment option for selected patients.
title: Totally endoscopic mitral valve replacement: reasons for non-feasibility of repair and 5-year outcomes.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patent foramen ovale (PFO), a common congenital atrial septal abnormality, can induce intracardiac right-to-left shunt (RLS) and is a potential risk factor for migraine. Currently, there is no unified consensus regarding the therapeutic efficacy and specific molecular mechanisms of PFO closure in the treatment of migraine.
METHODS: A single-center retrospective cohort study was conducted, enrolling 107 patients with PFO and migraine, of whom 58 underwent transcatheter PFO closure (observation group) and 49 received standard medical therapy (control group). All patients underwent cardiac imaging and contrast-enhanced transthoracic echocardiography before treatment, with follow-up assessments of headache episodes and scale scores at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-treatment. Simultaneously, peripheral arterial blood samples were collected from 5 PFO patients before and after surgery and from 5 healthy controls for plasma proteomic analysis, and changes in arterial partial pressure of oxygen and oxygen saturation were monitored.
RESULTS: The improvements in Visual Analogue Scale (VAS), Headache Impact Test (HIT-6), Migraine Disability Assessment (MIDAS), and Migraine-Specific Quality of Life Questionnaire (MSQ v2.1) scores at each follow-up time point were greater in the observation group than in the control group (all P < 0.05). At the 12-month follow-up, the overall treatment effective rate was 94.83% in the observation group, higher than 73.47% in the control group, with a statistically intergroup difference (P = 0.003). Stratified efficacy analysis revealed a higher proportion of markedly effective cases and a lower proportion of ineffective cases in the observation group, with statistically differences in the distribution of markedly effective and ineffective cases between groups (P < 0.05). Postoperative arterial partial pressure of oxygen and oxygen saturation were markedly improved compared with preoperative levels. Proteomic analysis suggested that the expression levels of inflammation-oxidative stress-related proteins, represented by myeloperoxidase (MPO), lysozyme C (LYZ), and heat shock protein 60 (HSPD1), were downregulated after surgery, and these changes appeared to be associated with the alleviation of hypoxia after elimination of intracardiac shunting.
CONCLUSIONS: PFO closure improved migraine symptoms in appropriately selected patients and was associated with downregulation of inflammation-oxidative stress proteins (MPO, LYZ, HSPD1). These findings provide preliminary molecular insights warranting further validation in larger cohorts.
title: Preliminary exploration of the pathogenesis of patent foramen ovale-related migraine and efficacy analysis of PFO closure.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Severe aortic stenosis is one of the most prevalent valvular heart diseases in the ageing population, and transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has become an effective and less invasive therapeutic alternative. Anatomical, pathophysiological, and clinical differences between women and men may influence outcomes following the procedure. This study aimed to evaluate the association between sex and mortality and procedure-related complications after TAVI in a real-world cohort from the Vigo Health Area.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-center observational study including 1,065 patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent transfemoral TAVI between 2010 and 2023. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality at 1 year. Secondary endpoints included bleeding, vascular complications, and new permanent pacemaker implantation. Time-to-event analyses were censored at 365 days; multivariable models used complete-case analysis.
RESULTS: Women were older and had greater frailty and higher surgical risk scores than men. In-hospital and 1-year mortality were similar between sexes. Date-based 30-day mortality was 2.4% in men and 3.7% in women (p = 0.225), and female sex was not independently associated with 30-day mortality after adjustment for age and STS score (adjusted OR 1.79, 95% CI 0.80-3.98; p = 0.154). Female sex was not independently associated with 1-year mortality (adjusted HR 1.07, 95% CI 0.69-1.66; p = 0.772). Women had more bleeding in unadjusted analyses, but female sex was not significantly associated with any bleeding after adjustment (adjusted OR 1.61, 95% CI 0.92-2.81; p = 0.093). Male sex remained associated with higher odds of new permanent pacemaker implantation (adjusted OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.03-2.17; p = 0.036).
CONCLUSIONS: Sex was not independently associated with short- or 1-year mortality after TAVI. Women had a higher unadjusted incidence of bleeding, whereas men had a higher incidence of new permanent pacemaker implantation that persisted after adjustment. These findings describe sex-related differences in procedural risk profiles but should be interpreted in the context of the observational design and the long study period.
title: Sex differences in clinical outcomes after transcatheter aortic valve implantation: a real-world cohort.

abstract: Berberine (BBR) has been demonstrated to exert cardiovascular protective effects by regulating lipids and ameliorating inflammation. Recent studies reported the interaction between BBR and gut microbiota in various metabolic diseases due to its low bioavailability. However, few studies examine the effect of BBR on the gut microbiota in coronary artery disease (CAD) individuals. We hence conducted a parallel-controlled, regularly visited clinical trial with 23 stable CAD patients who recently underwent percutaneous coronary intervention and completed a 12-week BBR ± standard therapy treatment. The BBR intervention was associated with a directional improvement in endothelial function, enhanced levels of low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), and a reduction in circulating inflammatory mediators (IL-1α, IL-17, MCP-1, MIP-1β, and VEGF). Using metagenomics and metabolomic studies, we identified that bacterial signatures varied significantly with gradually increasing doses of BBR. These results showed that a specific group of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA)-producing bacteria, mainly Ruminococcus sp., Roseburia sp., and Anaerostipes hadrus, were elevated following the BBR intervention, which was also negatively correlated with inflammatory factors. Notably, regardless of the background standard therapy, BBR reshaped gut-microbiota-encoded aromatic amino acid catabolism: it selectively enriched the microbial L-dopa, 3-hydroxyphenylacetic acid, and phenylpropionic acid branches, which were anchored by increased abundances of dopamine β-monooxygenase, porA, and acdA genes. Overall, we investigated the role of BBR in regulating microbial metabolic alterations and vascular function. Targeted restoration of the gut microbiota may present a novel ecological approach for managing cardiovascular disease.
title: Berberine improves lipid levels, vascular function, and gut microbial-dependent metabolites in stable coronary artery disease patients.

abstract: Dressler syndrome, the delayed pericarditis after myocardial infarction remains firmly established in cardiological teaching, yet contemporary direct evidence specific to it is sparse. Its reported incidence has fallen markedly in the reperfusion era, while post-cardiac injury syndrome (PCIS) is now encountered chiefly after cardiac surgery and catheter-based procedures. These trends reflect a change in the clinical settings in which delayed post-injury pericardial inflammation is recognised, rather than evidence of a transfer of the same biological disease burden; incidence estimates across eras and procedures are not directly comparable. The historical anti-heart antibody framework does not, on its own, account for current observations. Randomised trials in predominantly idiopathic recurrent pericarditis show that colchicine and interleukin-1 (IL-1)-directed agents (anakinra, rilonacept, goflikicept) reduce recurrence, and experimental and human pericardial tissue data implicate the NLRP3 inflammasome. These data support an important role for innate immune signalling in pericarditis, but they do not establish IL-1 dependency in late post-infarction Dressler syndrome, and they do not exclude a contribution of adaptive immunity to amplification, persistence or recurrence. We grade the evidence at three levels-direct human PCIS data, data from other human pericarditis phenotypes, and experimental data-and stratify therapeutic evidence by phenotype and drug class, distinguishing colchicine, for which randomised prevention data exist in post-pericardiotomy syndrome, from IL-1 blockade, for which no PCIS-specific trial exists. We propose a pericardial injury-threshold model as a testable hypothesis in which clinical expression reflects the interaction of damage-associated molecular pattern load, the directness of pericardial and mesothelial exposure, and host inflammatory susceptibility, with adaptive responses acting as potential amplifiers. The model yields falsifiable predictions and identifies a key unanswered question: whether IL-1 inhibition during infarct healing is safe and effective. We outline a staged research programme, including a candidate two-tier research case definition requiring prospective validation, registry-based ascertainment, pericardial fluid immunophenotyping, inflammasome genetics, and phenotype-specific trials, including of emerging direct NLRP3 inhibitors.
title: Dressler syndrome and post-cardiac injury syndrome: an autoinflammatory framework for reappraising a seventy-year-old diagnosis: a state-of-the-art review.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Coronary artery ectasia (CAE) is characterized by diffuse coronary dilatation and increased thrombotic risk. In patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and CAE, the optimal antithrombotic strategy remains unclear. Previously, an exploratory trial suggested that the combination of antiplatelet monotherapy plus oral anticoagulation may reduce ischaemic events without increasing bleeding risk compared to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), although it was underpowered for definitive conclusions.
AIMS: The aim of this study is to evaluate the efficacy and safety of antiplatelet monotherapy plus direct oral anticoagulation compared with DAPT in patients with ACS and culprit-vessel CAE in a multicentre randomized setting.
METHODS AND RESULTS: OVER-TIME II is a multicentre, multinational, randomized, open-label clinical trial with 1:1 allocation comparing acetylsalicylic acid 100 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg vs. clopidogrel 75 mg plus rivaroxaban 15 mg daily. The study will include 326 patients with ACS and culprit-vessel CAE. Patients will be followed for 12 months. The co-primary efficacy endpoint is the time to first occurrence of a composite of cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, or repeat revascularization. The co-primary safety endpoint is the time to first occurrence of major or minor bleeding defined by the Bleeding Academic Research Consortium criteria. Secondary endpoints include individual components of the primary outcomes. Exploratory analyses will include genomic and transcriptomic profiling through DNA and RNA sampling to identify molecular signatures associated with thrombotic risk, treatment response, and clinical outcomes.
CONCLUSION: OVER-TIME II is designed to provide robust multicentre randomized evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of an anticoagulation-based strategy in patients with ACS and CAE, with the potential to contribute to future clinical research and guideline development.
REGISTRATION: NCT07511257. The trial is registered and publicly available on ClinicalTrials.gov and is currently actively recruiting patients.
title: OVER-TIME II trial: design and rationale of a multicentre randomized study evaluating antithrombotic strategies in patients with acute coronary syndrome and coronary artery ectasia.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Brucellosis remains an important zoonotic disease in endemic regions and has heterogeneous clinical presentations. Cardiovascular involvement is uncommon, with myocarditis representing a rare but potentially serious manifestation. Brucellosis-associated myocarditis may mimic acute coronary syndrome (ACS), creating diagnostic uncertainty when obstructive coronary artery disease is absent.
CASE SUMMARY: We report a case of probable brucellosis-associated myocarditis in a 27-year-old previously healthy man with recently diagnosed brucellosis who developed acute chest pain and dyspnea accompanied by ischemic electrocardiographic changes and marked troponin elevation. Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved biventricular systolic function without regional wall-motion abnormalities, significant valvular disease, or pericardial effusion. Coronary angiography demonstrated normal coronary arteries without obstructive disease, establishing a working diagnosis of myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries (MINOCA). In the absence of cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or endomyocardial biopsy, the suspected myocarditis etiology was supported by the temporal relationship with active brucellosis, dynamic biomarkers, and electrocardiographic changes, exclusion of obstructive coronary artery disease, and subsequent clinical recovery. Because antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory therapies were administered concurrently, the response cannot be attributed to either intervention alone. No relapse or recurrent cardiac symptoms occurred during six months of follow-up.
CONCLUSION: In endemic regions, brucellosis-associated myocarditis should be considered among infectious causes of myocardial injury with non-obstructive coronary arteries. MINOCA is a working syndrome rather than an etiologic diagnosis. When cardiac MRI or endomyocardial biopsy is unavailable, epidemiologic exposure, microbiologic data, serial biomarkers, ECG evolution, echocardiography, and coronary angiography may support a probable diagnosis while acknowledging residual uncertainty.
title: Probable brucellosis-associated myocarditis presenting as myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries: a case report.

abstract: We report a case of a 64-year-old man with biventricular dysfunction and a large left ventricular (LV) thrombus in whom endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) was suspected. Despite extensive evaluation for eosinophilic, autoimmune, infective, and haematological causes, no secondary aetiology was identified. He was managed with guideline-directed heart failure therapy and anticoagulation. His condition progressively deteriorated, and he died within a year, highlighting the diagnostic challenge of suspected EMF when characteristic imaging findings coexist with atypical features and definitive histological confirmation cannot be obtained, as well as the therapeutic challenges of this rare cardiomyopathy.
title: Suspected Endomyocardial Fibrosis With Extensive Left Ventricular Thrombus: A Diagnostic Dilemma.

abstract: Coronary atherosclerosis, driven by the interplay of lipid metabolic derangements and chronic inflammation, constitutes the pathological basis of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and has emerged as the leading cause of mortality among Chinese residents. In patients with acute coronary syndrome, subsequent events may arise from initially nonculprit coronary lesions that appear angiographically mild. Invasive coronary angiography, the conventional diagnostic reference standard, is inherently invasive and incapable of characterizing plaque biological properties. Meanwhile, traditional risk factors only enable crude risk stratification, resulting in a critical shortage of precise early clinical screening modalities. Multi-omics technologies enable comprehensive molecular profiling of the human organism and effectively address the limitations of conventional detection approaches. Nevertheless, existing investigations remain largely confined to single-omics analyses; candidate biomarkers lack validation in large independent cohorts, and substantial bottlenecks persist in clinical translation. This review evaluates the respective advantages and limitations of genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, lipidomics, and gut metagenomics in coronary atherosclerosis research. It elucidates the scientific value of integrated multi-omics analysis in dissecting pathogenic regulatory networks, unraveling gut-heart axis mechanisms, and identifying targets for precision therapy. Furthermore, it summarizes cutting-edge technological advances including single-cell multi-omics, spatial multi-omics, liquid biopsy, and AI-powered multi-omics integration, and compiles multi-omics risk prediction models developed on the basis of large-scale population cohorts. By bridging genetic susceptibility, cellular remodeling, peripheral molecular signatures, and plaque phenotypes, multi-omics integration can underpin early risk warning for high-risk populations, plaque subtyping, and therapeutic efficacy monitoring. Looking ahead, the establishment of standardized, multicenter prospective cohorts and the application of Mendelian randomization to infer causal relationships will be pivotal. These efforts are essential to translate multi-omics into a practical framework for comprehensive precision medicine across the entire continuum of coronary atherosclerosis.
title: Multi-omics in coronary atherosclerosis: mechanistic insights and advances in precision diagnosis and treatment.

abstract: Pill-induced oesophageal injury or pill oesophagitis typically presents with acute retrosternal pain, odynophagia, and dysphagia. While often self-limiting, cases may mimic acute coronary syndrome, food bolus, oesophageal perforation, and mediastinitis. Doxycycline is among the most commonly implicated medications. We report the case of a 32-year-old woman with severe mid-oesophageal ulceration secondary to doxycycline commenced for rosacea, managed at a rural Australian hospital. The histopathology finding of granulomatous inflammation was deemed reactive and secondary to severe ulceration, in the absence of infection or sarcoidosis. The patient was treated supportively with complete clinical and endoscopic resolution. Clinicians should consider pill oesophagitis in patients with acute retrosternal pain and odynophagia after starting doxycycline, and conservative management can be successful.
title: Severe Doxycycline-Induced Oesophagitis With Granulomatous Inflammation Managed in a Rural Australian Hospital: A Case Report.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Lung transplantation combined with pectus excavatum repair has been reported in selected patients with severe pectus excavatum to expand the restricted thoracic cavity and facilitate graft accommodation. However, the safe implementation of this surgical strategy may be challenging in patients with extensive pleural adhesions after repeated pleurodeses, because of the increased risk of postoperative bleeding and re-thoracotomy.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 15-year-old boy with interstitial lung disease, secondary pulmonary hypertension, severe pectus excavatum, and multiple prior bilateral pleurodeses underwent deceased-donor bilateral lung transplantation using a planned delayed chest closure (DCC) strategy. Preoperative CT showed marked thoracic deformity with a Haller index of 9.1 and a leftward mediastinal shift. Because extensive pleural adhesions were expected to complicate graft implantation and hemostasis and increase the risk of re-thoracotomy for postoperative bleeding, a 2-stage strategy consisting of planned DCC followed by pectus bar placement at definitive chest closure was established at the time of transplant listing in collaboration with an external pectus specialist. Bilateral lung transplantation was performed under venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support, followed by temporary chest closure. At the second-stage operation on POD 2, 2 pectus bars were placed, and additional graft volume reduction was performed, allowing definitive chest closure without hemodynamic compromise. The patient was discharged home on POD 69 without wound complications or implant-related infections.
CONCLUSIONS: This case suggests that lung transplantation may be feasible in carefully selected patients with severe pectus excavatum and extensive pleural adhesions, with appropriate multidisciplinary planning. A preplanned 2-stage strategy incorporating DCC and pectus bar placement at definitive chest closure represents a potential option for such complex cases.
title: Lung Transplantation with Planned Delayed Chest Closure in Severe Pectus Excavatum after Multiple Pleurodeses: A Case Report.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study aims to explore the clinical value of lncRNA CARMN in acute myocardial infarction (AMI) patients.
METHODS: The study subjects included 156 AMI patients and 59 healthy controls. The serum CARMN levels were detected by real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). The correlation between CARMN and myocardial injury markers, as well as cardiac ultrasound indicators by Pearson analysis. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression were employed to screen out the independent influencing factors for MACE in AMI patients, and a nomogram was constructed.
RESULTS: In patients with AMI, the serum CARMN level is decreased. CARMN level correlated with cTnI, CK-MB, Myo, LVEF. A total of 156 patients with AMI were enrolled and followed up for 6 months, among whom 60 patients experienced MACE. Lower CARMN levels were associated with a higher incidence of MACE. The AUC of the combined model for predicting MACE reaches 0.867, and the nomogram has good calibration and high clinical net benefit.
CONCLUSION: Serum CARMN combined with myocardial injury markers and ultrasound indicators, may help predict MACE risk in patients with AMI.
title: Circulating CARMN for acute myocardial infarction prognosis and its incremental effect when combined with conventional biomarkers.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Gemella species are rare causes of infective endocarditis, and accurate species identification can be challenging with routine diagnostic methods. We report infective endocarditis caused by a novel Gemella species, highlighting the diagnostic value of sequencing-based approaches for bacteria not registered in public databases and the risk of misclassification when novel species are not represented in reference databases.
CASE SUMMARY: A 55-year-old Japanese man presented with fatigue, anorexia, and altered mental status. Echocardiography revealed vegetations on the mitral and tricuspid valves with severe mitral regurgitation, and imaging demonstrated multiple systemic embolic events. Blood cultures grew gram-positive cocci that were initially identified as Gemella bergeri by matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry. The patient received antimicrobial therapy and underwent mitral valve replacement and tricuspid valve repair. Culture of the excised valve tissue was negative. Metagenomic sequencing of the valve vegetation detected a Gemella species distinct from G. bergeri. Genome assembly from sequencing data showed 94.5% average nucleotide identity with a reference G. bergeri genome, supporting classification as a novel species. Whole-genome sequencing of the blood culture isolate demonstrated near-complete concordance with the organism detected in the valve tissue. The patient recovered with a 6-week course of intravenous penicillin G after blood cultures became sterile.
CONCLUSION: This case demonstrates that rare Gemella infections may be misidentified by routine mass spectrometry. It underscores the importance of sequencing-based methods for accurate pathogen identification and highlights a diagnostic pitfall associated with database-dependent identification in infective endocarditis.
title: Infective endocarditis due to a novel Gemella species revealed by metagenomic sequencing.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Neurological outcome is key to extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) benefit. However, the prognostic relevance of early PIV dynamics after ECPR remains poorly characterized.
METHODS: We conducted an exploratory retrospective single-center study of 107 ECPR patients with at least three valid complete blood count (CBC) measurements within 24 h of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) pump-on. The primary outcome was an unfavorable neurological outcome at hospital discharge, defined as Cerebral Performance Category (CPC) 3-5. Latent class mixed models (LCMMs) were used to identify early pan-immune-inflammation value (PIV) trajectory groups, and multivariable logistic regression evaluated their association with the outcome. Incremental predictive performance was explored using leakage-controlled nested cross-validation in which trajectory modeling was repeated within each outer training fold.
RESULTS: Among 107 included patients, 53 had an unfavorable neurological outcome at hospital discharge. Two distinct early PIV trajectory patterns were identified in this selected cohort: a high-baseline decreasing class (n=68) and a low-baseline rising class (n=39). The low-baseline rising class had a significantly higher rate of unfavorable neurological outcome than the high-baseline decreasing class (69.2% vs 38.2%, P=0.004). In the fully adjusted model, the low-baseline rising trajectory was associated with significantly higher odds of unfavorable neurological outcome compared with the high-baseline decreasing trajectory (odds ratio 5.70, 95% confidence interval 1.73-18.81, P=0.004). In an internal exploratory comparison, adding the trajectory class to the clinical risk model increased the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve from 0.746 to 0.812, but the bootstrap 95% CI for the AUC increment crossed zero.
CONCLUSION: Two exploratory early PIV trajectory groups were identified in this selected cohort. The low-baseline rising pattern was associated with a higher probability of CPC-defined unfavorable neurological outcome at hospital discharge in this selected single-center cohort. Although trajectory information numerically improved internal predictive performance, the incremental improvement was uncertain and requires external validation.
title: Early Pan-Immune-Inflammation Value Trajectories are Associated with Unfavorable Neurological Outcomes After Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Inflammation contributes to plaque instability and adverse outcomes in acute coronary syndromes (ACS). The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) is an inexpensive inflammatory marker, but its prognostic value for in-hospital and postdischarge outcomes remains incompletely defined.
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the association of admission NLR with postdischarge mortality, in-hospital adverse events, and length of stay (LOS) in patients with ACS.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed adults with ACS in the CardioMining database (NCT05176769). Admission NLR was ln-transfor med and analyzed continuously and by quartiles. Associations with postdischarge all-cause mortality were assessed using multivariable Cox proportional hazards models with sequential adjustment and restricted cubic spline analyses. Secondary outcomes were evaluated using logistic and linear regression. Discrimination was assessed with the C-index, and interactions by sex, age (<75 vs. ≥75 years), and ACS type were explored.
RESULTS: Among 4927 patients (mean age: 66.0 ± 13.4 years; 24.3% female), higher admission lnNLR independently predicted all-cause mortality [hazard ratio: 1.372, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.266-1.488; P < 0.001]. Mortality increased across lnNLR quartiles [Q2 adjusted hazard ratio (aHR): 1.225, Q3 aHR: 1.551, Q4 aHR: 1.831; all P < 0.05], with lower Kaplan-Meier survival at higher quartiles. Restricted cubic splines supported a predominantly linear relationship. Adding lnNLR improved discrimination (ΔC-index: +0.0096). Higher lnNLR was associated with in-hospital adverse events (adjusted odds ratio: 1.849, 95% CI 1.530-2.236; P < 0.001) and longer LOS (adjusted β: 0.129, 95% CI: 0.107-0.151; P < 0.001).
CONCLUSION: Admission NLR independently predicts mortality, in-hospital complications, and longer LOS in ACS, supporting early risk stratification.
title: Neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio and clinical outcomes across the acute coronary syndrome trajectory: insights from the CardioMining Study.
Dual-imaging assessment of Hertz contact intravascular lithotripsy in a complex calcified lesion.

abstract: Coronary calcified nodules are an uncommon but important substrate for acute coronary syndromes, stent underexpansion, and recurrent target lesion revascularization. This consensus integrates pathologic, imaging, prognostic, and interventional evidence to guide practical decision-making. Intravascular imaging is essential for diagnosis, mechanism definition, and procedural optimization. Optical coherence tomography provides superior assessment of cap disruption and thrombus, whereas intravascular ultrasound remains valuable when contrast exposure or lesion crossing limits optical coherence tomography. Treatment should be tailored to lesion crossability, calcium distribution, and the need for mechanical scaffolding. No calcium-modification device or drug-eluting stent vs drug-coated balloon strategy has demonstrated consistent superiority. The proposed type IIa/IIb framework is hypothesis-generating and requires prospective validation. Calcified nodule-related target lesion failure should be managed by correcting the dominant mechanical mechanism before antiproliferative therapy. These recommendations emphasize individualized, imaging-guided percutaneous coronary intervention and identify priorities for prospective comparative research.
authors: Interventional Cardiology Council of the Asian Heart Society
title: Management of Coronary Calcified Nodules: A Position Statement.
