The proposed approach can help manufacturers in elaboration and manufacturing of new TAVI polymer devices design made of TPU and SEBS polymers for clinical applications.
title: Experimental study of TPU and SEBS additively manufactured leaflets for novel aortic valve polymer TAVI prosthesis.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: New-onset atrial fibrillation (NOAF) is a frequent and clinically significant comorbidity following primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) for ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), associated with increased mortality, stroke risk, and healthcare costs. Predicting NOAF in this setting remains challenging. This study aimed to compare the predictive performance of four risk scores-CHA2DS2-VASc-60, mC2HEST, Mayo-AF, and HATCH-in identifying patients at high risk of NOAF after primary PCI in STEMI.
METHODS: We conducted a single-center, retrospective cohort study at Shaoxing Central Hospital, including consecutive adults with STEMI who underwent primary PCI within 12 h of symptom onset between February 2020 and June 2025. Patients with a history of atrial fibrillation or other exclusions were excluded. The endpoint was NOAF within 1 year after PCI, documented by continuous inpatient telemetry, 12-lead ECG at discharge, and routine follow-up ECGs at 1, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. We compared the discriminative ability of the four scores using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and assessed their clinical utility through net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI).
RESULTS: A total of 1,175 patients were included in the final analysis. The incidence of NOAF within 1 year was 8.2% (n = 96). The mC2HEST score demonstrated the highest area under the ROC curve (AUC) for predicting NOAF (AUC = 0.786), followed by HATCH (AUC = 0.746) and CHA2DS2-VASc-60 (AUC = 0.739), while Mayo-AF had the lowest AUC (AUC = 0.736).Pairwise comparisons showed that mC2HEST significantly outperformed CHA2DS2-VASc-60 (ΔAUC = 0.046, p = 0.002).
CONCLUSIONS: Among the four risk scores evaluated, mC2HEST provided the best predictive performance for NOAF after primary PCI in STEMI patients. Its superior discriminative ability and significant integrated discrimination improvement suggest that mC2HEST could be a valuable tool for identifying high-risk patients who may benefit from intensified monitoring and early interventions. Future prospective, multicenter studies are warranted to validate these findings.
title: Which score best predicts new-onset AF after primary PCI in STEMI? Head-to-head assessment of four algorithms.

abstract:
AIMS: To evaluate the association between beta-blocker (BB) prescription and long-term all-cause mortality after acute coronary syndrome (ACS), and to assess whether this varies across the left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) spectrum.
METHODS AND RESULTS: We analysed ACS patients from the retrospective multicentre CardioMining study (NCT05176769). The primary analysis used inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and restricted mean survival time (RMST) derived from weighted Kaplan-Meier curves. RMST and survival differences were estimated at 1 and 5 years. A landmark analysis evaluated survival between years 1 and 5 among first-year survivors. Among 6049 ACS patients (age 66.8 ± 13.2 years; 74.9% male), 5107 (84.4%) were discharged on BBs. During a median 4.6-year follow-up, 1912 deaths (31.6%) occurred. Overall, the 1-year RMST difference associated with BBs was 6.3 days (95%CI 0.0 to 13.2), which attenuated further by 5 years (11.3 days, 95%CI -30.7 to 63.9). The largest 1-year RMST difference was observed among patients with LVEF ≤40% (18.8 days, 95%CI 1.1 to 37.4), whereas associations were smaller and non-significant among patients with LVEF 41-49% and LVEF ≥50%. At 5 years, confidence intervals crossed the null across all LVEF categories. Continuous LVEF analyses suggested greater short-term benefit at lower values, with progressive attenuation across the LVEF spectrum. Among 1-year survivors, no significant RMST differences were observed between years 1 and 5.
CONCLUSION: Discharge BB prescription was not associated with a clear long-term survival advantage after ACS in this large real-world cohort. Apparent associations were strongest at lower LVEF values and attenuated during longer follow-up.
title: Beta-blockers after acute coronary syndrome: insights across the ejection fraction spectrum.

abstract: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) is an uncommon non-atherosclerotic cause of acute coronary syndrome that can present as ST-elevation myocardial infarction (MI) and is particularly challenging because postoperative thrombosis and bleeding risks coexist. We report the case of a 44-year-old woman who underwent major abdominal oncologic surgery and developed a minor pulmonary embolism treated with anticoagulation. On postoperative day 4, she developed acute chest pain with ST-segment elevation. Emergency coronary angiography showed a long lesion involving the second diagonal branch, consistent with SCAD, with otherwise normal coronary arteries. She was managed conservatively. Her course was complicated by right JP drain-site bleeding, which required permanent heparin discontinuation and blood transfusion. This case illustrates SCAD as a cause of postoperative ST-elevation MI and the difficulty of balancing thrombosis and bleeding risk after major surgery.
title: Postoperative spontaneous coronary artery dissection after major abdominal oncological surgery: a case report.

abstract: Intravenous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy have transformed acute ischemic stroke (AIS) care, yet angiographic recanalization does not guarantee adequate tissue reperfusion or long-term functional independence. Brain cytoprotection has therefore expanded from neuron-centered rescue to preservation of the ischemic penumbra, neurovascular unit, blood-brain barrier (BBB), and microcirculation. Using a systems-immunology perspective, this clinically oriented narrative review examines ischemia-reperfusion injury as a dynamic network linking danger-associated molecular pattern sensing, microglia and astrocytes, circulating leukocytes, platelets and complement, endothelium and pericytes, cytokine signaling, edema, no-reflow, and regulated cell-death programs. We integrate classic and recent evidence for excitotoxic, redox and mitochondrial, inflammatory, barrier, microvascular, and cell-death targets; evaluate representative pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions; and distinguish negative primary endpoints from exploratory subgroup or surrogate signals. Confirmatory excitotoxicity trials have remained negative overall. Selected multitarget agents have shown benefit in specific Chinese populations, whereas immune-, edema-, and no-reflow-directed approaches have yielded stage-specific but inconsistent safety, imaging, and functional results. Statins, nitric oxide donors, and phosphodiesterase inhibition have plausible vascular or immunomodulatory actions, but available trials do not establish them as acute cytoprotective therapies. Future development should align the right mechanism, tissue phenotype, treatment time, exposure, target-engagement measure, and patient-centered endpoint, followed by multicenter preclinical testing and independent cross-regional clinical replication. This end-to-end framework reframes brain cytoprotection as precision modulation of a spatially and temporally evolving neuroimmune-vascular system rather than a single undifferentiated treatment class.
title: Brain cytoprotection in acute ischemic stroke in the reperfusion era: neuroimmune networks, clinical evidence, and translational barriers.

abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has made macrovessel reopening achievable in acute ischemic stroke, but angiographic success does not ensure effective tissue-level reperfusion or microvascular oxygen delivery. This narrative review examines endothelial glycocalyx dysfunction as a plausible blood-facing interface that may connect pre-existing cardiometabolic vulnerability with post-thrombectomy microvascular dysfunction. Targeted English-language literature from PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar through 30 April 2026 was synthesized, with emphasis on MT, impaired microvascular reperfusion (IMR), no-reflow, blood-brain barrier (BBB) and neurovascular-unit (NVU) biology, glycocalyx-related biomarkers, cardiometabolic risk, perfusion imaging, and microcirculatory rescue. The evidence base is heterogeneous and is explicitly separated into direct human MT/LVO evidence, indirect human biomarker or imaging evidence, experimental cerebral evidence, non-cerebral/cross-disease vascular evidence, and hypothesis-generating mechanistic inference. Ischemic priming, abrupt reperfusion, oxidative and inflammatory stress, complement activation, metabolic stress, distal embolization, device-endothelial trauma, and host vulnerability may converge on the luminal endothelial surface. Glycocalyx dysfunction may amplify leukocyte adhesion and capillary plugging, platelet adhesion and microthrombosis, impaired mechanosensing and nitric-oxide signaling, BBB destabilization, and heterogeneous capillary flow; however, direct causal proof in human MT is lacking. Circulating syndecan-1, heparan sulfate, and hyaluronan are therefore best interpreted as time- and compartment-dependent systemic signals rather than direct readouts of the cerebral glycocalyx. Post-EVT microcirculatory rescue trials show that downstream perfusion may remain therapeutically actionable, but they do not demonstrate glycocalyx repair as the operative mechanism. A practical translational strategy is to combine serial, compartment-annotated biomarkers with prespecified early perfusion/barrier imaging and tissue endpoints, while explicitly modeling cardiometabolic vulnerability and competing microvascular mechanisms. The glycocalyx framework should therefore be considered a testable network hypothesis rather than an established primary cause of post-thrombectomy no-reflow or futile recanalization.
title: Endothelial glycocalyx dysfunction in the setting of mechanical thrombectomy: a conceptual link between cardiometabolic vulnerability and microvascular reperfusion failure.

abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Coronary artery disease may occur without standard modifiable cardiovascular risk factors (SMuRFs), but the frequency and angiographic phenotype of such presentations in South Asian catheterization cohorts remain uncertain. We estimated registry-defined SMuRF-less frequency, tested alternative dyslipidaemia definitions, and compared angiographic phenotypes by SMuRF status.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, single-centre, registry-based cross-sectional analysis of 51,864 admissions with matched catheterization records at a Bangladeshi tertiary cardiac centre from 2005 to 2024. Admissions were classified as SMuRF-less when no qualifying hypertension, diabetes, smoking, or dyslipidaemia was documented or identified; dyslipidaemia reflected a documented diagnosis or qualifying lipid measurement. Documented-only and statin-inclusive definitions were sensitivity analyses. We calculated unadjusted prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
RESULTS: Under the primary definition, 3172 admissions (6.1%) were SMuRF-less, compared with 6.5% under the documented-only definition and 1.6% under the statin-inclusive definition. Among admissions with a classifiable angiographic phenotype, SMuRF-less admissions more frequently had normal coronary arteries (24.9% vs. 10.7%; PR, 2.34; 95% CI, 2.18-2.50) and less frequently had obstructive coronary artery disease (56.6% vs. 71.2%; PR, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.77-0.82). Among admissions with obstructive disease, multivessel disease was less frequent (49.6% vs. 57.8%; PR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.82-0.90), whereas recorded intracoronary thrombus was more frequent (5.3% vs. 3.2%; PR, 1.65; 95% CI, 1.33-2.04). Of 6635 ST-elevation myocardial infarction admissions, 355 (5.4%) were SMuRF-less; 318 (89.6%) had obstructive disease.
CONCLUSION: Registry-defined SMuRF-less admissions, reflecting absence of documented qualifying factors rather than prospectively verified biological absence, were uncommon, and their estimated frequency depended on risk-factor ascertainment. Although their recorded angiographic burden was generally lower, obstructive disease remained common, particularly in ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The absence of documented SMuRFs should not provide clinical reassurance. Prospective patient-level studies with standardized risk-factor assessment and longitudinal follow-up are needed.
first_author_country: Department of Cardiology Ibrahim Cardiac Hospital & Research Institute Dhaka Bangladesh
last_author_country: Department of Cardiology Ibrahim Cardiac Hospital & Research Institute Dhaka Bangladesh
title: Absence of Documented Standard Modifiable Cardiovascular Risk Factors Among Catheterized Admissions in Bangladesh: Frequency and Coronary Angiographic Phenotype in a 20-Year Registry Study.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although drug-coated balloons (DCBs) outperform drug-eluting stents (DESs) in the treatment of de novo small-vessel coronary lesions, no comparable studies are available for de novo large-vessel coronary lesions.
METHODS: This retrospective study examined 960 patients with de novo large-vessel coronary lesions (reference vessel diameter ≥3.0 mm) who underwent paclitaxel DCB angioplasty or DES implantation at Beijing Anzhen Hospital. The study endpoints included all-cause death, myocardial infarction (MI), stroke, and target vessel revascularization (TVR). Kaplan-Meier (KM) curves and Cox regression analysis were used to investigate the clinical outcomes of patients in the DCB and DES groups.
RESULTS: The overall incidence rates of major adverse cardiac and cerebrovascular events (MACCEs), all-cause death, MI, stroke, and TVR were 9.27% (89/960), 1.5% (14 patients), 0.9% (9 patients), 0.6% (6 patients), and 6.8% (65 patients), respectively. No significant differences were observed between the DCB and DES groups in MACCEs (13.2% vs. 5.6%; p = 0.511), all-cause death (1.9% vs. 1.0%; p = 0.763), MI (0.6% vs. 1.2%; p = 0.239), or stroke (0.6% vs. 0.6%; p = 0.361). However, the TVR rate was significantly higher in the DCB group than in the DES group (10.1% vs. 3.6%; p = 0.028), and this difference persisted after multivariate adjustment.
CONCLUSIONS: For patients with de novo lesions in target vessels with diameters ≥3.0 mm, the safety and efficacy of DCB therapy were comparable to those of DES therapy, except for target vessel revascularization.
title: Outcomes of Drug-Coated Balloon Versus Drug-Eluting Stent for the Treatment of Large De Novo Coronary Lesions.

abstract: Pure native aortic regurgitation (AR) remains a challenging and frequently undertreated valvular disease, associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Surgical aortic valve repair or replacement remains the standard of care; however, many patients are older, frail, or at prohibitive surgical risk, creating an unmet need for less invasive therapeutic options. In this context, transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) has progressively emerged as a potential alternative. However, the application of TAVI in AR has historically been limited by the absence of annular and leaflet calcification, the presence of large and often noncircular annuli, and the resulting risks of transcatheter valve embolization or migration, residual paravalvular regurgitation, and conduction disturbances. This review summarizes contemporary evidence on TAVI for pure native AR, spanning early off-label experience with first-generation self-expanding and balloon-expandable valves to newer-generation platforms and dedicated devices. Recent observational studies and multicenter registries have shown meaningful improvements in procedural success, lower rates of residual AR and second valve implantation, and acceptable short- and mid-term mortality with contemporary off-label devices. Dedicated systems, including JenaValve Trilogy, J-Valve, and others, have further enhanced anchoring and sealing performance, achieving markedly lower rates of valve migration and significant residual regurgitation. Nonetheless, permanent pacemaker implantation remains a major limitation for several platforms. In parallel, the AURORA trial introduced an anatomy-guided strategy based on multidetector computed tomography classification and dual anchoring theory, suggesting that careful anatomical selection and optimized implantation planning may improve outcomes even with non-dedicated devices. Overall, TAVI has become a viable option for selected high-risk patients with severe symptomatic pure native AR and has now been incorporated into contemporary guidelines in this setting. Future progress will likely depend on further refinement of dedicated devices, reduction of conduction-related complications, and broader integration of patient-specific anatomical and biomechanical assessment to optimize device selection and implantation strategy.
title: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Implantation for Pure Native Aortic Regurgitation: A Comprehensive State-of-the-Art Review.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Simultaneous occlusion of two coronary arteries during ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) is rare and often associated with hemodynamic instability and poor prognosis. Identification of predisposing factors is crucial for prevention and risk stratification. A 53-year-old man with no classic cardiovascular risk factors other than smoking presented with inferoposterior STEMI complicated by syncope. Emergency coronary angiography revealed simultaneous occlusion of the proximal right coronary artery and distal left circumflex artery. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention was successfully performed in both vessels using intravascular imaging guidance. Subsequent evaluation demonstrated markedly elevated lipoprotein(a) levels (88 mg/dL) in the absence of other thrombotic or inflammatory disorders. Multimodality imaging revealed lipid-rich, macrophage-infiltrated plaques in multiple coronary arteries. Intensive lipid-lowering therapy achieved plaque stabilization during follow-up. This case suggests that elevated lipoprotein(a) may be associated with simultaneous multivessel coronary thrombosis and could contribute to plaque vulnerability and thrombogenicity, highlighting the importance of aggressive lipid management.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE: Simultaneous multivessel coronary occlusion is a rare but life-threatening presentation of ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction. This case illustrates that markedly elevated lipoprotein(a) may be associated with widespread plaque vulnerability, emphasizing the importance of considering lipoprotein(a) measurement and intensive lipid-lowering therapy even in patients without traditional cardiovascular risk factors.
title: Simultaneous two-vessel occlusion causing ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction associated with elevated lipoprotein (a): A case report.

abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the last remaining conduit in a patient with severely impaired left ventricular function is among the most hazardous procedures in contemporary interventional cardiology, as any interruption of flow essentially constitutes a global ischemic insult. We describe a 77-year-old man, a former heavy smoker with an 80-pack-year smoking history, who had undergone three-vessel coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) 22 years previously. His medical history also included chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, severe heart failure with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 25-30%, and severe mitral regurgitation (MR). At presentation, he had Canadian Cardiovascular Society class III angina and New York Heart Association class III symptoms. The most recent coronary angiogram, performed 6 months earlier, demonstrated chronic total occlusion (CTO) of both saphenous vein grafts, in addition to CTO of all three native epicardial coronary arteries. Thus, the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) graft to the left anterior descending artery (LAD) represented the sole functional conduit, directly perfusing the LAD territory and supplying the right coronary and circumflex territories through primarily septal and epicardial collaterals, respectively. The LAD displayed two sequential severe stenoses (≥80% each), one at the distal LIMA-LAD anastomosis and another further distally in the native vessel. In accordance with current coronary revascularization guidelines, the Heart Team recommended evaluation by cardiac surgeons. Two independent cardiothoracic surgeons declined redo CABG as a viable therapeutic option. Complex and high-risk indicated PCI (CHIP) was therefore considered the only feasible revascularization strategy. Additional hemodynamic support with percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (pMCS) was deemed necessary. Residual MR and arrhythmic risk, including the potential indication for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD), were planned to be reassessed 3 months after successful percutaneous revascularization. CHIP was performed under full hemodynamic support with a continuous-flow microaxial pump (Impella CP with SmartAssist) inserted via the left femoral artery, while coronary intervention was performed through the ipsilateral radial artery using a 6-F IMA guiding catheter. The lesions were successfully crossed with a workhorse wire, despite substantial technical difficulty and with the aid of a microcatheter; however, distal flow was immediately lost, and intracoronary nitroglycerin failed to restore it. Balloon angioplasty restored flow only partially, and a decision was made to proceed with stent implantation. However, stent delivery proved challenging, requiring a guide-extension catheter to be advanced deep into the LIMA body using the so-called 'inchworming technique.' Despite successful implantation of the first drug-eluting stent (DES) at the distal anastomotic lesion, a second DES could not be advanced to the more distal native LAD lesion, despite the use of multiple guidewires and supportive guiding-catheter strategies. Therefore, a drug-coated balloon (DCB) was used as a bailout strategy, immediately restoring TIMI grade 3 flow and leaving only a minor, non-flow-limiting type B dissection. Impella support was discontinued early because of access-related left lower-limb ischemia, and successful percutaneous hemostasis was achieved using a suture-based closure technique. Peak high-sensitivity troponin I, measured the following evening, was 10,800 pg/mL. The patient was discharged ambulatory on day 2 and remained asymptomatic at 3-month follow-up, when an ICD was implanted for primary prevention. This case illustrates the critical role of pMCS in maintaining hemodynamic stability when native coronary flow is lost during PCI of the last remaining conduit and highlights the value of DCB angioplasty as a bailout strategy when stent delivery is not feasible.
title: Case Report: Impella CP-protected percutaneous coronary intervention of the last remaining vessel-a LIMA-to-LAD graft-complicated by no-reflow and rescued with a drug-coated balloon.

abstract: Type 2 diabetes is associated with accelerated coronary atherosclerosis, recurrent ischemic events, and impaired vascular healing after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI); however, the effects of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists across these distinct coronary outcomes remain incompletely characterized. This systematic review synthesized randomized evidence on myocardial infarction (MI), acute coronary syndrome (ACS), coronary revascularization, post-PCI healing, and mechanistic markers of coronary disease. MEDLINE via PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) were initially searched for eligible reports published from January 1, 2020, through December 31, 2025. All four database searches were updated on August 31, 2026, extending publication eligibility through that date; no additional eligible reports were identified. The review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement. Seven eligible reports derived from seven parent randomized trials, involving 37,033 participants, were included. Two presented primary findings from independent randomized trials, three were prespecified analyses of parent randomized trials, and two were post hoc analyses. Owing to substantial clinical and outcome heterogeneity, the findings were synthesized narratively. Albiglutide reduced first and recurrent MI, including type 1 and type 2 events, whereas higher-dose efpeglenatide yielded more favorable cardiovascular effect estimates than the lower dose. Across separate reports, semaglutide favorably modified epicardial adipose tissue, a surrogate imaging measure, and reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, MI, or stroke in patients with diabetic kidney disease. Liraglutide was associated with lower risks of broader cardiovascular composites compared with the other glucose-lowering therapies combined, although individual MI and revascularization outcomes were not significantly reduced. Exenatide did not significantly reduce the composite of hospitalization for ACS or coronary revascularization, and the only PCI-specific trial demonstrated no significant improvement in early stent coverage, neointimal thickness, or in-stent obstruction. Of the seven included reports, one was judged to have a low risk of bias, whereas six raised some concerns, primarily because of post hoc analyses, open-label treatment, incomplete methodological reporting, or limited imaging follow-up. Across the included reports, findings were more favorable for MI and broader cardiovascular events than for coronary revascularization or post-stent healing. However, the small number of heterogeneous reports, reliance on several secondary or post hoc analyses, and absence of quantitative meta-analysis limit firm conclusions and do not establish a definitive class-wide coronary effect. Potential differences by agent, dose, and patient phenotype require further investigation, while treatment-initiation timing remains largely untested.
title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists Across the Coronary Disease Continuum in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review of Ischemic Events, Revascularization, and Stent Healing.

abstract: Non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) associated with cholangiocarcinoma is rare, with only a few case reports described. The diagnosis is usually made after a thrombotic event or stroke. We report the case of a 44-year-old South African woman who presented with cardiogenic shock and ST elevation while receiving rivaroxaban for a recent pulmonary embolism. Autopsy revealed myocardial embolization secondary to NBTE associated with cholangiocarcinoma. This case highlights the value of point-of-care echocardiography in ruling out complications or alternative diagnoses in atypical presentations of acute coronary syndrome. Furthermore, it underscores that, in NBTE, anticoagulation with heparin is the preferred regimen.
title: Non-bacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis Presenting as Cardiogenic Shock With Anterior ST Elevation Revealing an Occult Cholangiocarcinoma: A Case Report.

abstract:
AIMS: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used by the public and healthcare professionals for clinical reasoning. However, they were developed as general-purpose language models rather than dedicated clinical decision-support tools, and their performance in real-world acute heart failure (AHF) management remains insufficiently evaluated. We compared four contemporary AI models with physician decision-making.
METHODS AND RESULTS: This single-centre retrospective observational study incorporated a cross-sectional AI evaluation of consecutive patients treated at Sotiria General Hospital between July and November 2025, excluding acute coronary syndrome. ChatGPT, ChatGPT Plus, DeepSeek, and an ESC guideline-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) model independently assessed identical standardized cases. Recommendations were compared with physician decisions on diagnosis, treatment, guideline-directed medical therapy, timing, and prognosis using Cohen's kappa, McNemar's test, Cochran's Q, Wilcoxon signed-rank testing, and multivariable logistic regression. Diagnostic performance differed significantly across systems (Cochran's Q = 8.477, P = 0.037). In the balanced diagnostic cohort, ChatGPT Plus achieved the highest heart failure (HF) accuracy (accuracy 86.5%, sensitivity 87.0%, and specificity 86.0%), followed by RAG (accuracy 77.5%), ChatGPT (accuracy 77.0%), and DeepSeek (accuracy 69.0%). For HF within the top three differential diagnoses, sensitivity was 90.0-97.0%; specificity was 70.0% for ChatGPT Plus, 68.0% for RAG, 19.0% for DeepSeek, and 15.0% for ChatGPT. Physician agreement was highest for guideline-directed therapies, with greater variability in prognosis and escalation of care. RAG more closely matched physician therapeutic timing but did not consistently outperform general-purpose models.
CONCLUSION: Contemporary AI models show promise in AHF decision support but substantial task-specific variability, supporting use as complements rather than replacements for physician judgement.
title: Artificial intelligence versus physician decision-making in acute heart failure: a comparative evaluation of four contemporary AI systems.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sepsis-induced myocardial injury (SIMI) is a severe complication with high mortality, yet effective prognostic prediction tools remain limited. Although platelet-derived indices have been explored in SIMI, these metrics primarily reflect systemic inflammation rather than the extent of myocardial injury or metabolic status.
METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 3071 critically ill individuals with SIMI admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) General Hospital between January 2020 and October 2025. The association between the platelet count (PLT)/lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) ratio and in-hospital mortality was assessed using multivariable Cox regression, restricted cubic splines, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Subgroup analyses evaluated consistency across clinically relevant strata.
RESULTS: The PLT/LDH ratio was independently associated with lower in-hospital mortality (hazard ratio [HR] = 0.44, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.34-0.57, p < 0.001). Compared with the lowest tertile, the highest tertile of PLT/LDH ratio was associated with a 67% reduction in risk (HR = 0.33, 95% CI: 0.25-0.43, p < 0.001). The PLT/LDH ratio demonstrated modest, statistically significant incremental discriminative performance over PLT or LDH alone (both p < 0.05). A nonlinear relationship was observed, with an inflection point at approximately 0.306 (p for nonlinearity < 0.0001). Subgroup analyses revealed a consistent association across all subgroups, with significant interactions for sex, hypertension, chronic kidney disease, and liver disease (all p for interaction < 0.05).
CONCLUSIONS: The PLT/LDH ratio is independently associated with in-hospital mortality in patients with SIMI. It may serve as a simple and practical tool for prognostic prediction in patients with SIMI upon ICU admission.
title: Association Between Platelet Count/Lactate Dehydrogenase Ratio and In-Hospital Mortality in the Patients With Sepsis-Induced Myocardial Injury.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: To compare the incidence of stroke at 1 and 2 years following transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) versus surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR), aiming to inform clinical decision-making regarding the safety and effectiveness of these interventions.
METHODS: A random-effects meta-analysis was conducted including 9 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 9865 patients. The primary endpoint was the incidence of stroke at 1 and 2 years post-procedure.
RESULTS: At 1 year, TAVR was associated with a lower incidence of stroke compared with SAVR (odds ratio (OR), 0.77; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.61-0.98; p = 0.03). No significant difference was observed at 2 years (OR, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.65-1.17; p = 0.37).
CONCLUSIONS: TAVR significantly reduces the risk of stroke within 1 year post-procedure compared with SAVR; however, this effect was not maintained at 2 years. These findings highlight the early benefit of TAVR, while the long-term advantage requires further investigation.
THE PROSPERO REGISTRATION: This study has been registered with PROSPERO, registration number: CRD42025636191, https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42025636191.
title: Risk of Short-Term Stroke in Non-High-Risk Patients Undergoing Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement vs Surgical Aortic Valve Replacement: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

abstract: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) is the most common acute coronary syndrome presentation and represents a heterogeneous clinical entity with distinct mechanisms and distinct diagnostic and therapeutic implications. This narrative review summarizes contemporary concepts in NSTEMI pathophysiology, classification, angiographic phenotypes, and treatment strategies, with an emphasis on differentiating Type 1 from Type 2 myocardial infarction (MI) and the implications for revascularization decisions. The PubMed/MEDLINE database was searched for English-language publications addressing NSTEMI pathophysiology, classification, diagnosis, and management, supplemented by the most recent American and European acute coronary syndrome guidelines, the Universal Definition of Myocardial Infarction, landmark randomized controlled trials, and pivotal mechanistic and intravascular imaging studies, with priority given to contemporary and high-impact sources. NSTEMI emerges as a heterogeneous syndrome rather than a single disease, and optimal care depends on identifying the underlying mechanism. This requires distinguishing myocardial infarction from myocardial injury, separating Type 1 atherothrombosis from Type 2 supply-demand mismatch, and recognizing entities such as myocardial infarction with non-obstructive coronary arteries and spontaneous coronary artery dissection. A mechanism-specific approach should guide antithrombotic therapy and revascularization decisions, and the transition from a syndromic label to an individualized, mechanism-based diagnosis is essential for optimizing patient outcomes.
title: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction.

abstract: Historically considered a "neglected" valvular disease, moderate-to-severe tricuspid regurgitation (TR) is now recognized as an important contributor to morbidity, mortality, and right-sided heart failure (HF). Natural history studies show that significant TR is frequently associated with left-sided valve disease, particularly mitral valve disease, and independently predicts poor outcomes as severity increases. The 2025 European Society of Cardiology (ESC)/European Association for Cardio-Thoracic Surgery (EACTS) Guidelines for the Management of Valvular Heart Disease place unprecedented emphasis on TR, elevating this condition from a secondary afterthought to a central element of comprehensive valvular therapy. This reflects an evolution of evidence over the past decade, underscored by increased diagnostic sensitivity through multimodal imaging and the development of novel therapeutic options. However, gaps in the existing evidence persist, and addressing these uncertainties will support future research. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the evidence on TR, incorporates updates from the latest European guidelines, focuses on the most relevant and controversial aspects of patient selection, and identifies key areas where knowledge is insufficient. Furthermore, this review revisits the historical foundations of tricuspid valve research, highlighting how several anatomical concepts fundamental to contemporary interventions were already described as early as the 17th century, underscoring the long-standing scientific interest in this once "forgotten" valve.
title: Tricuspid Regurgitation, the Once-Forgotten Valve: Current Management Options and Remaining Gaps After the 2025 European Society of Cardiology Guidelines Update.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Sinus tachycardia is common after acute myocardial infarction (AMI), but persistent tachycardia disproportionate to clinical status may worsen hemodynamics. We report a case of refractory sinus tachycardia associated with hemodynamic deterioration following AMI that responded to ivabradine. A 57-year-old woman developed cardiogenic shock due to anterior myocardial infarction and underwent emergency percutaneous coronary intervention with mechanical circulatory support. During recovery, she developed persistent sinus tachycardia exceeding 120 bpm, accompanied by worsening pulmonary congestion and increased pulmonary artery wedge pressure. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm with gradual warm-up and cool-down patterns, without abrupt onset or termination, suggesting inappropriate sinus node-mediated tachycardia. Beta-blockers were avoided because of hypotension and ongoing inotropic support. Ivabradine was initiated, resulting in prompt heart rate reduction and improvement in hemodynamics, including decreased pulmonary artery wedge pressure and improved left ventricular filling. Dobutamine may have contributed to the tachycardia; however, the persistent and disproportionate nature of the sinus tachycardia suggested enhanced sinus node automaticity. This case highlights that inappropriate sinus node-mediated tachycardia may contribute to hemodynamic deterioration after AMI and that ivabradine can be an effective therapeutic option when beta-blockers are not tolerated.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE: Disproportionate sinus tachycardia can occur even during the acute phase of myocardial infarction and may worsen hemodynamic status. When sinus tachycardia persists despite correction of reversible causes and appears excessive relative to the clinical condition, inappropriate sinus node-mediated tachycardia should be considered. Ivabradine may be an effective therapeutic option when beta-blockers are not suitable.
title: Ivabradine for inappropriate sinus node-mediated tachycardia associated with hemodynamic deterioration after acute myocardial infarction: A case report.

abstract: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) is a widely used technology in cardiac surgery practice. A clinically significant yet underexplored presentation that occurs during peripheral femoro-femoral venoarterial ECMO (VA-ECMO) is differential hypoxemia (DH) or Harlequin syndrome. This phenomenon may occur when the aortic mixing interface shifts distally, and the coronary and supra-aortic circulations receive predominantly hypoxemic native blood. DH may reduce cerebral and myocardial oxygen delivery and produce clinically meaningful arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) gradients. This scoping review aimed to synthesize clinical and experimental evidence on the mechanisms, detection, management, and outcomes of DH during peripheral VA-ECMO. A scoping review of the watershed phenomenon during peripheral VA-ECMO was conducted using MEDLINE and EMBASE in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. The initial search identified 245 records. After screening, 16 studies were included. DH frequency ranged from 1.5% to 13.3%, but estimates varied substantially across case definitions, diagnostic thresholds, and cohort compositions. Regarding management, configuration-targeted strategies improved surrogates of upper-body oxygenation and perfusion, which included shifting venous drainage toward the superior vena cava/upper right atrium, in turn converting to veno-arteriovenous ECMO with internal jugular return (with flow-splitting control) and relocating arterial return to more proximal/antegrade sites. Detection extended beyond paired upper- and lower-body oximetry/arterial blood gases; reported approaches included contrast-enhanced ultrasound, Doppler mapping, and positional computed tomography angiography (CTA). Experimental models described why DH may persist despite higher ECMO flow as native output increases, and they highlight anatomy- and cannulation-dependent cerebral and coronary vulnerability. DH appears to be a predictable, physiology-driven complication best mitigated by modifying drainage position and/or circuit configuration rather than increasing ECMO flow. To further explore this phenomenon, adopting standardized definitions, investigating bedside localization tools, and conducting prospective comparative studies could be considered.
title: The Aortic Watershed Phenomenon and Differential Hypoxemia During Peripheral Venoarterial ECMO: A Scoping Review of Clinical and Experimental Evidence.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Immediate coronary reperfusion is the cornerstone of therapy for acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), aiming to limit myocardial damage. Traditionally, the development of pathological Q waves on the electrocardiogram (ECG) has been considered a marker of irreversible transmural myocardial injury. However, most data on the incidence of pathological Q waves originate from the thrombolytic era. Therefore, the incidence and clinical significance of pathological Q waves in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within the currently recommended time window remain unclear, as does the overall relationship with clinical outcomes.
METHODS: This study included 116 patients with STEMI who underwent PCI. In accordance with the current European Society of Cardiology guidelines, treatment was initiated within the recommended 90 minutes after admission.
RESULTS: Pathological Q waves developed in approximately 14% of patients, a lower incidence than that reported in the thrombolytic era. Pathological Q waves were more frequent among older patients, those with a lower baseline left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), and those with a longer time interval between admission and PCI. After adjustment for multiple variables, the presence of new pathological Q waves was not associated with an increased rate of one-year readmissions.
CONCLUSIONS: In patients with STEMI undergoing PCI within the recommended time window, the incidence of pathological Q waves is substantially lower than that reported in the thrombolytic era and does not appear to be associated with a higher risk for readmissions. Further larger studies are warranted to confirm these findings.
title: Incidence and Implications of Q Waves After Acute ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction in the Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Era.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Cardiac involvement is a major cause of morbidity in hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES). We report a rare case of severe mitral regurgitation (MR) associated with HES in which apparent echocardiographic regression after imatinib therapy masked irreversible structural disease. A 63-year-old man presented with progressive exertional dyspnea and heart failure caused by severe MR. Marked eosinophilia led to the diagnosis of a myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with PDGFRB rearrangement. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed infiltrative thickening of the posterior mitral leaflet with vegetation-like subvalvular structures. Imatinib therapy rapidly normalized eosinophil counts, and follow-up echocardiography demonstrated disappearance of the vegetation-like structures; however, MR persisted. Because of progressive symptoms, mitral valve replacement was performed. Intraoperative findings revealed firm fusion of the posterior mitral leaflet and subvalvular apparatus to the left ventricular wall. The postoperative course was uneventful. This case highlights that apparent regression of valvular lesions after imatinib therapy does not necessarily indicate reversibility of structural disease in HES.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE: To understand that hypereosinophilic syndrome can cause irreversible subvalvular fusion leading to persistent mitral regurgitation despite adequate medical therapy, including imatinib. This case highlights the importance of careful echocardiographic evaluation of subvalvular involvement and timely consideration of surgical intervention when structural valvular damage progresses.
title: Persistent mitral regurgitation due to subvalvular fusion in hypereosinophilic syndrome despite imatinib therapy.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is an established treatment option for stroke prevention in patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) who are unsuitable for long-term oral anticoagulation. However, an anatomically challenging left atrial appendage (LAA) can limit optimal device positioning and complete occlusion with conventional fixed-curve sheaths.Two elderly men with NVAF and high bleeding risk underwent LAAC using Watchman FLX Pro devices (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA). Pre-procedural imaging revealed anatomically challenging LAAs. With a standard double-curve sheath, one case showed unacceptable posterior protrusion of a large 40-mm device. In another case, tilting of the device led to incomplete coverage of the posterior lobe, resulting in a residual peri-device leak. After switching to the TruSteer™ Access System (Boston Scientific), a bidirectional steerable sheath, improved coaxial alignment, enabled acceptable device protrusion, complete sealing with no residual leak, and stable device release in both cases. These cases suggest that a steerable sheath can overcome the limitations of fixed-curve sheaths in anatomically challenging LAAs by enabling coaxial alignment and optimized posterior wall apposition during LAAC.
LEARNING OBJECTIVE: In wide-neck, shallow, or multilobed left atrial appendages (LAAs), failure to meet PASS criteria with a conventional fixed-curve sheath may reflect non-coaxial deployment and, with very large devices, sheath instability due to kick-back at release, leading to device tilt. A bidirectional steerable sheath provides real-time control of the delivery axis and may prevent kick-back at release, enabling reproducible optimal device positioning in anatomically challenging LAAs where fixed-curve sheaths are inadequate.
title: Feasibility of steerable sheath-guided left atrial appendage closure in challenging anatomy.

abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is increasingly recognized as an episode of care that extends well beyond hospital discharge. Current guidance is distributed across several documents: the 2019 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines; the 2026 American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology (AHA/ACC) multisociety guideline, which replaced the massive/submassive terminology with clinical categories A-E; and separate position papers on catheter-directed intervention (CDI) and on follow-up. This narrative review (i) provides a side-by-side comparison of the ESC and AHA/ACC risk frameworks and their therapeutic implications; (ii) updates the evidence on reperfusion, including the recent randomized trials HI-PEITHO, PEERLESS and STORM-PE; and (iii) focuses on transitions of care and long-term follow-up, which guidelines address less comprehensively. Anticoagulation, preferably with a direct oral anticoagulant, remains the treatment for most patients. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk (ESC) or category E (AHA/ACC) PE, because in intermediate-risk disease it halves hemodynamic decompensation at the cost of a several-fold increase in major and intracranial bleeding, without long-term functional benefit. In HI-PEITHO, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced a 7-day composite outcome driven by cardiorespiratory decompensation (4.0% vs. 10.3%) in intermediate-high-risk patients with additional markers of physiological stress, without intracranial hemorrhage; a survival benefit of CDI has not been demonstrated. At discharge, a minimum bundle should specify the drug, dose, anticipated duration, provoking context, bleeding mitigation and follow-up ownership, followed by early contact within one week and a structured review at approximately three months. Up to half of survivors report persistent dyspnea or exercise limitation, whereas chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) develops in approximately 2%-3%. Persistent symptoms should prompt phenotype-directed evaluation with echocardiography, ventilation/perfusion scintigraphy, cardiopulmonary exercise testing and, when indicated, right-heart catheterization interpreted with the 2022 hemodynamic definitions, followed by early referral to an expert center where pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and medical therapy can be combined. We state the type of evidence underpinning each key recommendation, propose a discharge bundle, a structured follow-up algorithm and episode-wide quality indicators, and identify the evidence gaps that should guide future trials.
title: Integrated management of acute pulmonary embolism and the post-pulmonary embolism syndrome: risk stratification, modern therapies, and long-term follow-up.

abstract: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) exposes the hypertrophied myocardium to cardioplegic arrest in the setting of increased left ventricle (LV) mass, interstitial fibrosis, impaired relaxation, coronary microvascular dysfunction, and reduced perfusion reserve. These abnormalities may increase susceptibility to ischemic injury and complicate homogeneous cardioplegic delivery. This focused narrative review synthesizes physiological and clinical evidence on cardioplegia composition, temperature, delivery route, dosing, redosing, and myocardial protection during prolonged aortic cross-clamping in adults undergoing surgical aortic valve replacement. AS-specific comparative studies remain limited, generally small, and frequently reliant on biochemical markers; meanwhile, larger observational cohorts and contemporary randomized aortic valve replacement (AVR) trials also vary substantially in patient selection and myocardial protection protocols. Although some studies have associated cold blood cardioplegia with lower biomarker release than cold crystalloid cardioplegia, and cold maintenance strategies with less biochemical injury than warm cardioplegia, no formulation, temperature, or delivery route has demonstrated consistent superiority in clinically important outcomes. Limited historical evidence also suggests that body weight-based dosing may inadequately reflect myocardial requirements in marked LV hypertrophy, but no validated LV mass-based regimen currently exists. Therefore, cardioplegia in severe AS should be considered within a comprehensive myocardial protection protocol incorporating composition, temperature, dose, delivery route, redosing strategy, myocardial phenotype, associated valve or coronary disease, and anticipated cross-clamp duration. Prospective AS-specific studies using standardized protocols, LV mass stratification, and clinically meaningful outcomes are required.
title: Cardioplegia Strategies in Aortic Stenosis: A Focused Review of Current Evidence for Surgical Considerations.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Aorto-ostial de novo coronary lesions (AOL) represent a technically challenging subset of coronary artery disease with historically high restenosis rates, even with contemporary drug-eluting stent (DES) platforms. Drug-coated balloons (DCB) offer a stent-less alternative strategy; however, data on their use in AOL are limited. We aimed to compare long-term clinical outcomes of DCB vs. DES in de novo AOL.
METHODS: We identified all patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with either DCB or DES for de novo AOL as their first procedure between January 2015 and November 2019. The primary endpoint was target lesion failure (TLF), defined as a composite of target lesion revascularisation (TLR), target lesion myocardial infarction (TLMI), and cardiovascular death. Secondary endpoints included the individual components of TLF, target vessel revascularisation and all-cause mortality. Exploratory quantitative coronary angiography (QCA) analysis was performed on any follow up angiograms obtained that were technically feasible. Clinical outcomes were obtained using national outcome datasets.
RESULTS: A total of 197 patients with aorto-ostial lesions were included (DES n = 140; DCB n = 57). Over a median follow-up of 3.7 years, TLF occurred in 17.1% of DES-treated lesions and 14.0% of DCB-treated lesions (HR: 0.79, 95% CI: 0.35-1.76; p = 0.563). Rates of TLR, TVR, TLMI, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality were similar between groups. Severe calcification and creatinine independently predicted TLF. Follow-up QCA was available in 59 lesions over varying time intervals and demonstrated lower late lumen loss (LLL) following DCB treatment, compared with DES-treated lesions.
CONCLUSION: In this real-world cohort with aorto-ostial coronary lesions, a DCB-only strategy was feasible and associated with similar long-term outcomes to DES. Exploratory angiographic analyses demonstrated significant late lumen gain following DCB treatment. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further prospective evaluation of a DCB approach in aorto-ostial coronary disease.
title: DCB vs. DES in aorto-ostial lesions- clinical outcomes and QCA insights from SPARTAN registry.

abstract: Managing nonvalvular atrial fibrillation (NVAF) in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and prior embolism is challenging. This retrospective study evaluated long-term outcomes of left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO) compared with oral anticoagulation (OAC) and antiplatelet therapy (APT) in primary (n = 647) and external validation (n = 570) cohorts. The primary composite outcome included recurrent ischemic stroke or systemic embolism, major bleeding, and all-cause mortality. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), risks of the primary outcome, major bleeding, and mortality for LAAO were comparable with or lower than those of OAC and APT. For recurrent embolism, competing-risk analyses showed both OAC (SHR = 3.578, p = 0.003) and APT (SHR = 2.494, p = 0.040) carried a higher risk than LAAO. Results were consistent in the external validation cohort. These findings suggest LAAO may be a reasonable option for this high-risk population, offering a lower risk of recurrent embolism and comparable risk of major bleeding relative to pharmacological therapies.
title: Left atrial appendage occlusion versus antithrombotic therapy in nonvalvular AF with ASCVD and prior embolism.

abstract: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) has historically been considered the "forgotten valve disease", but growing evidence has established its independent prognostic impact and has driven the rapid expansion of transcatheter tricuspid valve interventions. While transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair (T-TEER) has demonstrated safety and clinical benefit in patients with secondary functional TR, evidence supporting its use in primary TR remains scarce, and surgery continues to represent the standard treatment. However, many patients with primary TR are considered ineligible for surgery because of prohibitive operative risk, creating an important unmet therapeutic need. In this Perspective, we discuss the potential role of T-TEER in selected patients with primary TR through the paradigm of a patient who developed torrential TR following iatrogenic rupture of the septal papillary muscle-chordal apparatus during cardiac device lead extraction. Owing to multiple comorbidities and prohibitive surgical risk, the patient underwent successful transcatheter repair with two PASCAL Ace devices, achieving durable TR reduction and sustained clinical improvement at one-year follow-up. Building on this experience, we review the current evidence supporting transcatheter tricuspid interventions, discuss the anatomical and procedural considerations that may enable T-TEER in selected forms of primary TR, and highlight the limitations of the available literature. We propose that carefully selected anatomical subsets of primary TR may represent an emerging frontier for transcatheter therapies, bridging the gap between guideline-directed management and individualized treatment when surgery is not feasible. Prospective studies are warranted to define patient selection criteria, procedural feasibility, and long-term clinical outcomes.
title: Salvaging the forgotten valve: T-TEER as the new frontier in torrential primary TR.

abstract: Calcific aortic stenosis (CAVS) is the most prevalent valvular heart disease affecting older adults, yet no validated pharmacological intervention can halt its progressive deterioration. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] denotes a genetically regulated low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-like particle, in which apolipoprotein(a) forms a covalent bond with apolipoprotein B-100. Cumulative genetic, epidemiological, imaging and mechanistic research supports a causal role for elevated circulating Lp(a) in the initiation, and suggests a contribution to the advancement, of calcific aortic valve lesions. Lp(a) mediates valve injury mainly via preferentially transporting oxidized phospholipids (OxPL), anchoring within aortic valve leaflets, triggering endothelial activation and inflammatory cascades, as well as stimulating the autotaxin-lysophosphatidic acid (ATX-LPA) axis; collectively these signals drive osteogenic differentiation and mineralization of valve interstitial cells (VICs). Higher Lp(a) levels correlate with incident aortic valve calcification, accelerated hemodynamic deterioration, augmented calcium deposition quantified by computed tomography (CT), and elevated risks of aortic valve replacement (AVR) or all-cause cardiac death. Conventional lipid-lowering agents fail to reverse disease trajectory in patients with established CAVS. Though proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors only modestly cut Lp(a) concentrations, exploratory analyses have delivered preliminary suggestive signals for cardiovascular protection. RNA-targeted therapeutics and oral agents blocking Lp(a) assembly can reduce circulating Lp(a) by 70% up to over 95%, as demonstrated in early- and mid-phase clinical trials. Most notably, the ongoing Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS randomized trial is directly testing whether pelacarsen can decelerate CAVS progression, and no completed trial has yet demonstrated that Lp(a) lowering modifies CAVS disease. This narrative review summarizes Lp(a) biological characteristics, causal evidence linking Lp(a) to CAVS, together with opportunities and unresolved uncertainties surrounding Lp(a)-targeted therapeutic strategies.
title: Lipoprotein(a) in calcific aortic stenosis: mechanistic insights, clinical evidence, and emerging therapies.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were developed to address some limitations associated with permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES), but the comparative safety and efficacy of these scaffolds remain uncertain.
METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and observational studies comparing BVS with contemporary DES in patients with coronary artery disease. The primary outcome was the composite clinical endpoint at 1-year. Secondary outcomes included mortality, myocardial infarction (MI), revascularization, thrombosis, and angiographic measures. Outcomes at 2, 3, and 5 years were analyzed separately. Trial sequential analysis (TSA) was used to assess the robustness of the evidence for the primary outcome.
RESULTS: A total of 51 studies (69 reports) were included. At 1 year, BVS was associated with a higher risk of the composite clinical endpoint than DES (risk ratio (RR) 1.11, 95% confidence interval (CI 1.00-1.22)), mainly driven by increased risks of MI, target lesion revascularization, and thrombosis. In contrast, all-cause and cardiac mortality did not differ significantly between groups. TSA showed that although the cumulative Z-curve reached the required information size, the Z-score did not cross the trial sequential monitoring boundary, indicating that the evidence for the primary endpoint remained inconclusive. During mid- and long-term follow-up, BVS remained associated with higher risks of ischemic events and repeat revascularization, without a survival benefit. Angiographic analyses showed greater late lumen loss, smaller minimal lumen diameter, and greater diameter stenosis with BVS.
CONCLUSIONS: Compared with contemporary DES, BVS appears to confer a higher ischemic risk without a long-term mortality benefit. Contemporary DES remains the preferred revascularization strategy.
title: Efficacy and Safety of Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds Versus Contemporary Drug-Eluting Stents in Coronary Artery Disease: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis.

abstract: Transradial access has become the preferred approach for percutaneous coronary angiography and intervention, largely because this technique reduces vascular complications, bleeding, costs, and patient discomfort compared with transfemoral access. However, anatomical variation, access site difficulties, procedural complications, and other factors can limit success. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the anatomic basis of transradial access, including radial artery anatomy, patient and access site selection, procedural considerations, complications, and emerging applications. This review also highlights key clinical trial data supporting the benefits of transradial access and discusses future directions in technique and technology. Our goal is to provide a practical, comprehensive resource for successful use of this approach.
title: Transradial Coronary Angiography and Intervention: Current Concepts and Future Directions.

title: Rational and design of the FREESCA study: A multicenter prospective study assessing the prognostic value of continuous glucose monitoring during hospitalization for acute coronary syndrome.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Elevated systemic immune-inflammation index (SII) correlates with increased coronary artery disease (CAD) prevalence and severity in acute coronary syndrome (ACS). The aim of this study was to evaluate the influence of sex on SII and its association with coronary stenosis in ACS.
METHODS: A total of 130 patients with ACS, who had performed coronary angiography, were enrolled. Gensini Score (GS) was used to reflect the degree of coronary stenosis. The association of SII and GS were studied.
RESULTS: The mean values of SII and GS were significantly higher (p = 0.048 and 0.001, respectively) in male individuals compared with female counterparts. There was a significant correlation between SII and GS (r = 0.306, p = 0.006) in male participants. However, the positive correlation between SII and GS was not found in female subjects. SII was independently associated with GS (B = 0.030, p = 0.007) after controlling for age, smoking, and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) in male participants. LDL-C (B = 11.741, p = 0.003), smoking (B = 39.018, p = 0.016) and age (B = 1.139, p = 0.030), but not SII (B = 0.027, p = 0.101) were found to be independently correlated with the degree of coronary stenosis in females.
CONCLUSIONS: SII was a associated marker for evaluating the extent of coronary lesions in male subjects with ACS, but not in female counterparts.
title: Sex Differences in the Association Between the Systemic Immune-Inflammation Index and Coronary Lesion Severity in Acute Coronary Syndrome.
